Duif works in the Delft group built around SESANS , a technique that measures structure in real space over a range from nanometres to tenths of a millimetre without the tight collimation that ordinary small-angle scattering requires. The trick is to encode the scattering angle in the Larmor precession of the neutron's spin rather than in its position on a detector, which allows a wide beam and so a much larger usable flux.

GRAVIMAGRETISM represents Part IV of Marinov's encyclopaedic CLASSICAL PHYSICS. In Marinov's absolute space-time theory the gravitational phenomena are considered by analogy with the electromagnetic phenomena. Aiming to obtain a complete mathematical similarity in the gravitational and electromagnetic theories, Marinov introduces hypothetically the magretic energy as a space-time companion to the space gravitational energy, in the same manner as magnetic energy is a space-time companion to the space electric energy. For this reason Marinov re-names the gravitational theory "gravimagretism. Until today experiments have not given proofs about the existence or non-existence of magretic energy. Such an experiment (the "cauldron" experiment) is proposed by Marinov in Part V. The results of Marinov's accelerated "coupled-mirrors" experiment (described in Part III) shows that Einstein's principle of equivalence is not valid, i.e. one can make an experimental distinction between a kinematic and a gravitational acceleration. Marinov's high-velocity experiments lead to the conclusion that our universe is static as a whole. Thus Marinov considers the "red shift" of the galaxies as a gravitational effect and not as a Doppler effect due to the "escaping velocities" of the galaxies. Marinov shows that the gravitational treatment of the "red shift" leads to a quadratic dependence on the distance to the galaxies and not to a linear dependence as one obtains at the Doppler treatment. The observational data fit better to a quadratic dependence and not to a linear dependence as was established previously by Hubble.

Both the classical and the relativistic composition law for velocities are applied to re-calculate the Sagnac Effect. The ensuing formulae for the fringe shift are found to differ already in first order of v/c. Whilst the classical formula is validated by interferometric measurements and verified by the GPS-system, this is not the case for the relativistic result.
Overview
Wolfgang Engelhardt, retired from the Max-Planck-Institut für Plasmaphysik at Garching, published this short 2013 paper arguing that special relativity, correctly applied, predicts no Sagnac effect — and that since the effect is measured and is used in GPS, the theory's basic postulate is at stake.
The argument is set out in two parallel derivations. Section 2 treats the rotating interferometer classically. Adapting the Galilean transformation to a circular path by writing d s ′ = d s − v ₀d t with d t ′ = d t , he obtains the composition law v φ ′ = v φ − v ₀, and hence travel times L /( c ∓ v ₀) for the two beams and the standard fringe shift ΔZ = 4 A · Ω / cλ ₀. He notes that Michelson and Gale verified this in 1925 by varying the enclosed area, and reads the result as showing "an 'ether wind' must exist due to the rotation of the earth".
Section 3 repeats the exercise with the Lorentz transformation. Writing the differential form d t ′ = γ(d t − v ₀d s / c ²) and d s ′ = γ(d s − v ₀d t ), and dividing, he obtains the relativistic composition law
v φ ′ = ( v φ − v ₀)/(1 − v φ v ₀/ c ²)

The Special Relativity Theory (SRT) and the General Relativity Theory (GRT) sometimes exhibit clock effects of equal magnitude which cancel and sometimes exhibit clock effects of equal magnitude which are additive. This cannot be coincidence, yet there is nothing within the two disjoint relativity theories to suggest an underlying mechanism. The effects appear to be related to energy, but the SRT treats energy as relative and the GRT treats an orbiting body as following a force-free trajectory. Following a brief review of MLET concepts, it is contrasted with SRT concepts. Current data available from a number of modern experiments are evaluated with regard to both MLET and SRT. In general, MLET provides a more coherent and consistent explanation of the data. In the principal section of the paper it is shown that in the earth-centered inertial (ECI) frame Global Positioning System (GPS) clocks must not be adjusted for the gradient of the sun's gravitational potential. MLET shows that the differential effect of the sun's gravitational potential is absorbed into the clock bias which converts the Selleri transformation into an apparent Lorentz transformation. By contrast, there is no valid explanation for this phenomenon which is consistent with SRT/GRT and they are thereby refuted. Cláudio Nassif (also published as Cláudio Nassif Cruz ) is a Brazilian theoretical physicist working at the Centro Brasileiro de Pesquisas Físicas and in Belo Horizonte, who has developed over two decades a modification of special relativity called Symmetrical Special Relativity (SSR).
Its central idea is a single, elegant addition. Special relativity has an unattainable maximum speed, c . Nassif adds an unattainable minimum speed, V — equally invariant, equally a barrier — so that the range of possible speeds becomes the doubly bounded interval V < v ≤ c instead of 0 ≤ v < c .
The consequence is that rest is abolished . No particle can be at rest, because rest would require v = 0, and V cannot be reached. And since the minimum speed must be the same for all observers, it defines a privileged frame — which means SSR breaks Lorentz symmetry .
Nassif is distinguished among the researchers catalogued on this wiki by his publication record. His work has appeared in Physics of the Dark Universe , General Relativity and Gravitation , the International Journal of Modern Physics D , Pramana , Modern Physics Letters A and the Canadian Journal of Physics — mainstream refereed journals, over some thirty papers.

The name states the programme's premise: that physical theory should be answerable to ordinary standards of intelligibility — that every effect has a cause, that objects have definite properties whether or not anyone is observing them, and that a model which cannot be pictured is not yet an explanation. Its founding claims are that the universe and all natural phenomena are fundamentally electrical in character , and that matter is best described using geometric models set in absolute time and Galilean space .
CSS is unusual among alternative-physics efforts in three respects: it produced a sustained, multi-decade research programme rather than a single thesis; it published a regular quarterly journal, Foundations of Science , for more than twenty years; and it is openly and explicitly grounded in a Christian creationist worldview , which its members regard as the source of the realist and causal commitments that classical physics once shared and modern physics abandoned.

Abstract
There are two competing formulations of time in physics. Newton defended in the Principia the utilization of absolute time which, according to him "flows equably without relation to anything external." Leibniz, on the other hand, was against this concept and proposed relative time to replace it: "As for my opinion, I have said more than once, that I hold space to be something merely relative, as time is; that I hold it to be an order of coexistences, as time is an order of successions." Leibniz's ideas were accepted and developed by Ernst Mach in his book The Science of Mechanics . Mach proposed to replace Newton's absolute time by the angle of rotation of the planets relative to the frame of fixed stars. In this work we consider the implementation of relational time and its consequences for physics. We concentrate our analysis in a single phenomenon, namely, the flattening of the Earth due to its diurnal rotation. We consider the figure of the Earth in Newtonian mechanics. We point out some philosophical problems with this classical formulation. We then present the flattening of the Earth from the point of view of Relational Mechanics, which is a mathematical implementation of Mach's principle utilizing Weber's law for gravitation.

Coriolis force is the sideways deflection experienced by a body moving within a rotating system — the apparent curving of winds and ocean currents on the spinning Earth being the standard example. It acts at right angles to the body's velocity and to the rotation axis, and in textbook mechanics it takes the form 2 m Ω × v , where m is the mass, Ω the angular velocity of the frame, and v the body's velocity within it. The expression was written down by the French engineer Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis in an 1835 paper on the energetics of rotating machinery such as water wheels, where he called it the compound centrifugal force .
Like centrifugal force , its companion, the Coriolis force is classed in modern mechanics as a fictitious or inertial force: a term that appears in the equations only when motion is described from a rotating frame, with no physical agent behind it. That classification is the point of dispute in the literature archived on this wiki, and this page follows the same division as the centrifugal-force article — the standard account first, then the objections raised by the researchers here.
The mainstream account
Newton's first law holds that a body free of net force moves in a straight line at constant speed. Seen from a frame rotating at angular velocity Ω , that straight-line motion appears curved, and the equations of motion acquire two extra terms to preserve the form of Newton's second law: a centrifugal term directed outward, proportional to Ω², and a Coriolis term, proportional to Ω and to the body's velocity, acting perpendicular to its motion.
On the orthodox reading these are bookkeeping devices, not forces. They have no agent and no reaction partner, and they vanish when the description is returned to an inertial frame. title: Cosmic Microwave Background
content_preview:
The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is a faint, extremely uniform bath of microwave radiation arriving from every direction in the sky, with a spectrum very close to that of a blackbody at about 2.725 K. In standard cosmology it is interpreted as relic radiation released when the expanding universe first became transparent to light, roughly 380,000 years after the Big Bang .
It was found accidentally in 1964–65 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson at Bell Telephone Laboratories in Holmdel, New Jersey, who could not eliminate a persistent excess antenna temperature of a few kelvin from their horn reflector at 7.35 cm. Their brief 1965 announcement in the Astrophysical Journal appeared alongside a companion paper by Robert Dicke, Jim Peebles, Peter Roll and David Wilkinson interpreting the signal cosmologically. Penzias and Wilson shared the 1978 Nobel Prize in Physics. The COBE satellite's FIRAS instrument showed in 1990 that the spectrum matches a blackbody to remarkable precision, and COBE's DMR instrument detected in 1992 the temperature anisotropies — variations of order one part in 100,000 — whose statistics were later mapped in detail by WMAP and by Planck. Superimposed on this is a much larger dipole, at the millikelvin level, attributed to the motion of the solar system relative to the radiation field.
Within the standard model the CMB is the single most quantitatively powerful cosmological dataset: the angular power spectrum of its fluctuations is what fixes most of the parameters of the concordance model, including the Hubble constant and the density attributed to dark matter and dark energy .
A note on prediction
The CMB is usually presented as a successful prediction of the hot Big Bang, and Ralph Alpher, Robert Herman and George Gamow did estimate a present-day relic temperature of a few kelvin in the late 1940s. The cosmological constant , written Λ (lambda), is a term Einstein added to the field equations of general relativity in 1917 to permit a static universe, later discarded, and revived at the end of the twentieth century as the standard description of dark energy .
Einstein's original difficulty was that his field equations, applied to a uniform distribution of matter, gave no static solution: gravity would cause the whole to collapse. Λ supplied a uniform repulsion, tuned to balance the attraction exactly. The balance is unstable, as Arthur Eddington pointed out, and the motivation disappeared when the redshift –distance relation was published in 1929 (see Hubble Constant ). Einstein dropped the term; George Gamow later reported that Einstein had called it his greatest blunder, though the phrase survives only at second hand.
Λ returned in 1998, when two supernova survey teams reported that distant Type Ia supernovae are dimmer than a decelerating universe predicts, and concluded that cosmic expansion is accelerating. Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess shared the 2011 Nobel Prize. In the resulting concordance model — ΛCDM — the constant accounts for roughly 68 per cent of the total energy density, with cold dark matter and ordinary matter making up the rest.
The cosmological constant problem
Λ is mathematically equivalent to a uniform energy density of the vacuum with negative pressure, and this identification produces the largest quantitative failure in physics. Estimating the vacuum energy of quantum fields by summing zero-point contributions up to a natural cut-off gives a number exceeding the cosmologically inferred value by many tens of orders of magnitude — the figure of 120 orders is often quoted, and even the most conservative estimates leave a discrepancy of dozens of orders. This Natural Philosophy wiki page disputes content found on Wikipedia page wikipedia:Cosmology
Cosmology is the study of the universe as a whole — its structure, its history, and on the standard account its origin. It is the branch of physics in which the ratio of theory to observation is highest, and the branch this wiki disputes most comprehensively.
Category: Cosmology catalogues nearly 700 items. This page is a map of that literature; the arguments themselves are set out on the topic pages linked from it.
For Hermann Bondi's 1952 monograph of this name, see Cosmology (Bondi book) .
Cosmology or cosmogony?
A distinction drawn repeatedly in this literature is worth taking first, because it frames everything else. Cosmology is the study of the universe; cosmogony is the study of its origin. Glenn Borchardt argues that the two have been conflated, and that the second is not a legitimate scientific subject at all:
IUT denies that cosmogony, the study of the origin of the universe, is legitimate. The word "cosmogony" has not seen popular use in cosmology. To do so would imply that an alternative view was possible. … The creation of something from nothing is clearly a religious assumption, not a scientific one.
— Glenn Borchardt, "Infinite Universe Theory" (2007)
On that view the question is not which origin story is correct but whether an origin story is required. The alternative — an Eternal Universe , infinite in space and time — dissolves the problem rather than solving it, and is the position of a large part of the literature here.
The standard model and its critics
The mainstream account is the Big Bang : an expanding universe some 13.8 billion years old, beginning hot and dense, with structure growing under gravity from primordial fluctuations. Its principal supports are the redshift–distance relation, the cosmic microwave background, and the abundances of the light elements.

Cosmology is a monograph by the cosmologist Hermann Bondi , first published in 1952 by Cambridge University Press (reprinted 1960) in the Cambridge Monographs on Physics series.
Overview
Written soon after the term "Big Bang" was coined, the book aimed to establish cosmology as a distinct branch of physics . Bondi surveys the basic principles and the observational evidence, and reviews the cosmological theories of the day — Newtonian and general-relativistic cosmologies, the theories of Eddington, Dirac, and Jordan, Milne's kinematic relativity, and the steady-state theory (which Bondi himself co-created). For many years it was the standard introductory survey of the subject.
About the author
Sir Hermann Bondi (1919–2005) was an Austrian-British mathematician and cosmologist, best known as a co-author (with Thomas Gold and Fred Hoyle) of the steady-state theory of the universe. See also his Assumption and Myth in Physical Theory and the volume The Nature of Time , from a meeting he convened with Gold.

Gravity draws galaxies into clusters, which grow by accretion and collision until a dominant central galaxy emerges — invariably, he says, a spiral with an active nucleus, and the most dominant of these are Seyferts. When a critical mass and density are reached in the central region, the Seyfert's core undergoes a transformation producing quasar precursor masses, which are ejected in opposite directions along the poles, perhaps by magnetic repulsion. Following Halton Arp, the ejected quasars grow fuzzy as they travel and evolve into ordinary galaxies, which in time are drawn back into clusters and the cycle repeats.
The starting point is philosophical rather than observational. Wright takes Existence as "a self-evident fact, as an axiomatic concept that cannot be refuted," and argues that "if we would rule out magic, we must conclude that existence exists everywhere," so the ocean of galaxies extends in every direction to infinity and has neither beginning nor end. title: Natural Philosophy Wiki
content_preview:
Coulomb's law states that the electrostatic force between two point charges acts along the line joining them, is proportional to the product of the charges, and falls off as the inverse square of their separation: F = k q ₁ q ₂⁄ r ². It is the foundation of electrostatics and, for most of the researchers catalogued on this wiki, the one piece of classical electrodynamics nobody wants to change.
The standard account
Charles-Augustin de Coulomb published the law in 1785, having measured the force with a torsion balance of his own design. Henry Cavendish had established the inverse-square dependence more precisely a decade earlier, by a null method — showing that no charge resides on the inner of two connected concentric spheres, which holds only if the exponent is exactly 2 — but did not publish, and the result became known only when Maxwell edited his papers a century later.
The null method remains the basis of the modern tests, and they are extraordinarily tight: modern experiments constrain any departure of the exponent from 2 to less than about one part in 10¹⁵. The same experiments are read as an upper bound on the photon rest mass, since a massive photon would give a Yukawa-type exponential cutoff rather than a pure inverse square.
In the standard formulation Coulomb's law is a special case, not an axiom: it is what Gauss's law — the first of Maxwell's equations — gives for a static point charge, and it is the low-velocity limit of the full electrodynamic interaction. The law as written applies to charges at rest; once charges move, the standard theory says that the electric force is supplemented by a magnetic one, and the whole is expressed by the Lorentz force law .
The inverse-square form has a structural consequence worth noting: it makes the electrostatic self-energy of a genuine point charge infinite. Classical electrodynamics has never resolved this, and it is renormalised away rather than answered in quantum electrodynamics.

Abstract
The cross antenna is a medium gain and circular polarization structure made of a conductor or strip line over a ground plane, following a cross contour of four or more branches. One end is feed by a generator and the other one is charged with a load impedance. This paper presents a theoretical and experimental analysis of an eight arms cross antenna, loaded with four different impedances. The theoretical study is made via the computational solution of Pocklington's equation applied to the structure; experimental results are obtained over an antenna of a 12 AWG wire over a ground plane, working in 3.2 GHz. We present radiation efficiency, gain, field pattern, and axial rate results.

This is an ordinary applied- electromagnetics engineering paper rather than a foundational one, and it should be read as such: it appeared in Apeiron but takes no position on any contested question in physics. The authors — J. Sosa-Pedroza, A. Lucas-Bravo and J. López-Bonilla of SEPI-ESIME-Zacatenco at the Instituto Politécnico Nacional in Mexico City — model and then build an eight-arm cross antenna operating at 3.2 GHz, and compare the computed radiation pattern against measurements taken in an anechoic chamber.
The motivation is that the cross structure is nearly unstudied. It belongs to the family of travelling-wave current-distribution antennas and was introduced by Antoine Roederer in an IEEE paper of 1990; the authors remark that "it seems that no other article has been written about the subject". Curtis E. "Curt" Renshaw (born 20 December 1957) is an American electrical engineer, defense contractor and independent relativity theorist. Over more than two decades he has developed a Galilean-Newtonian alternative to Einstein's special and general relativity, built on a "Radiation Continuum Model" of light that replaces Einstein's second postulate. Describing himself as a "philosopher-at-large," he is known for his work in the Philosophy of Science and on the nature of time and Consciousness , and in particular for his reappraisal of Aristotle's account of time as "the number of motion."
Biography
Jencka was born in 1956 in Detroit, Michigan. He began composing as a teenager and studied musical composition with the American composer Stanley Hollingsworth, who taught at Oakland University in Michigan. Jencka pursued undergraduate study of philosophy and music at Oakland University.

Work
Jencka's philosophical work centers on the problem of time. He revisits Aristotle's classical thesis, set out in the Physics , that time is not a thing in itself but rather "the number of motion" with respect to before and after. Jencka argues that this roughly 2,300-year-old account retains its explanatory power and carries consequences that challenge assumptions held both in everyday thinking and in modern science.

Dannel Roberts (also credited as Dannell Roberts ) is an independent theoretical physicist and inventor who has developed an alternative particle-based model of the atom that he calls the key ring atom . He is the author of Particle Mechanics: The Theory of Energy States , and presented his work in a sustained series of talks at the ExtraOrdinary Technology Conference between 2013 and 2017. He is not to be confused with the unrelated Jack Roberts documented elsewhere on this wiki.
Scientific contributions
The key ring atom
Roberts's work begins from a single universal particle that changes states, with each state having its own purpose and characteristics. From this he builds a mechanical, model-able picture of atomic structure — the key ring atom — which he uses in place of the conventional orbital picture to account for solids, liquids and gases, for chemical bonding, and for the properties of light. In his account of visible light, three particles with differing reflective and absorption properties are sufficient to explain the phenomenon. His book Particle Mechanics extends the same scheme to sound, electricity, magnetism, heat and cold, and introduces gravity "as a completely new concept."
Gravity shielding
Roberts's best-known claim, presented at the 2014 conference, is that gravitational shielding is achievable. He rejects the idea that gravity is a pulling force and argues instead that gravity is a particle that pushes — gravity particles stream toward and through an atom, so that interrupting the flow interrupts the effect. Wikipedia Dispute : wikipedia:Dark matter
This Natural Philosophy wiki page disputes content found on Wikipedia page wikipedia:Dark matter
Dark matter is the name given, in mainstream astrophysics, to a hypothetical form of matter that neither emits nor absorbs light and whose presence is inferred solely from its gravitational effects. It was introduced to close a gap in the accounts: galaxies and clusters of galaxies appear to move as though they contained far more mass than can be seen in stars, gas and dust. On the standard cosmological model dark matter accounts for roughly 85% of all matter, and together with dark energy for something like 95% of the total mass-energy of the universe — a figure which means that, on the orthodox account, the substance we can observe is a small residue of what is really there.
The literature collected on this wiki takes a very different view. Almost none of the researchers documented here accept dark matter as a substance. They regard it instead as an artefact — of a gravitational law misapplied, or of a gravitational law that is itself incomplete, or of forces other than gravity operating at galactic scale, or of a cosmology whose mass budget is wrong because its interpretation of redshift is wrong. What unites them is not a shared alternative but a shared diagnosis: that a discrepancy between prediction and observation was resolved by inventing the missing term rather than by re-examining the theory that generated it. As Tom Van Flandern put it, dark matter is the best known of the " ad hoc helper hypotheses" by which the standard model accommodates observations after the fact.
This article sets out the observational problem as the mainstream states it, then the distinct lines of objection found in the papers archived here, then the alternatives those researchers propose in its place.

Title Dark Matter: Early Considerations

Author(s) Jaan Einasto
Keywords Dark matter , galaxies, clusters of galaxies
Published 2004
No. of pages 18
Abstract
A review of the study of dark matter is given, starting with earliest studies and finishing with the establishment of the standard Cold Dark Matter paradigm in mid 1980-s. Particular attention is given to the collision of the classical and new paradigms concerning the matter content of the Universe. Also the amount of baryonic matter, dark matter and dark energy is discussed using modern estimates.
Overview
This is a historical review, written as a School lecture and circulated as astro-ph/0401341, in which Jaan Einasto traces the emergence of the Dark Matter concept from Ernst Öpik's 1915 estimate of the density of matter near the galactic plane to the acceptance of the Cold Dark Matter (CDM) model in the mid-1980s. Einasto is not a neutral chronicler: he was one of the principals. The 1974 Tartu paper of Einasto, Kaasik and Saar — which argued in Nature that all giant galaxies are surrounded by massive non-stellar "coronas" — is one of the two papers he identifies as having settled the question, the other being Ostriker, Peebles and Yahil (1974) from Princeton.
The review's organising claim is that dark matter was never "discovered" in a single observation. Einasto presents it explicitly as a Kuhnian paradigm shift: "as often in a paradigm shift, there is no single discovery, the new concept was developed step-by-step." He insists on separating two problems that are often conflated — local dark matter in the disk of our own Galaxy, and global dark matter around galaxies and clusters — and concludes that the first largely evaporated while the second did not. For a wiki whose contributors are frequently sceptical of dark matter, the chief value of the paper is that it is a first-hand account of how the case was actually assembled, including the objections raised against it at the time

David de Hilster will be discussing whether or not Dark Matter is real or a fantasy. Much time and energy are spent by both dissidents and mainstream scientists trying to find this elusive "stuff". But David's question is: does it exist or are we looking for a ghost? Join him live this Saturday!
Summary
David de Hilster on why he thinks dark matter is unnecessary, built around a scripted video of his own and two papers from the society, with a panel discussion after. He was frank about his motive: he keeps seeing dissidents discussing dark matter when, on his reading, the work refuting it has already been done, and he wanted to get it off his chest.
The argument
The claim is that the anomaly is an artefact of treating galaxies as point masses. The Keplerian fall-off in stellar velocity is derived for a spherical, uniform gravitational field; a spiral galaxy is flat and full of arms, and its field is nothing of the kind. Overlaying the one on the other and finding a discrepancy does not establish an unseen mass.
His strongest exhibit was the reports of galaxies without dark matter, which struck him when he first saw them: the two in question are spherical. Das Universum funktioniert anders – Realität kontra Relativität ("The Universe Works Differently – Reality versus Relativity") is a 1998 German-language book by the engineer Eduard Krausz , published by Corona Verlag. In it Krausz sets out his Alternative Gravitation Theory and argues that the foundations of nuclear physics and astrophysics are far less secure than they are usually presented to be.
Krausz's central claim is that gravity is not a fixed property tied to an object's mass but the effect of a physical medium — an aether he pictures as a kind of pressure wave streaming out of space and pushing bodies toward one another and toward a planet. On this view a fluid flows around and through all bodies and particles in proportion to their mass. He contends that such a model explains nuclear- and astro-physical phenomena more consistently and more plausibly than mainstream physics, which he regards as fixated on particles. The book connects this theory to his 1991 "Gelsenkirchen experiment," which he presented as evidence for the partial shielding of gravity.
Written for a general readership, the book sits at the border between physics and the wider critical debate over the aether and relativity . Its argument is not accepted by mainstream physics.

David Dameron is a researcher known for experimental and theoretical work on the Marinov Motor , a controversial electromagnetic device whose operation is claimed to be difficult to reconcile with the conventional Lorentz force law. He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Work
Dameron published "Flux Leakage Tests for the Marinov Motor" in the journal Apeiron (Vol. 7, No. 3–4, 2000), reporting a series of tests intended to evaluate the effect of magnetic flux leakage on the motor's behaviour. He concludes that leakage may play a significant part in the observed effect but does not fully account for the motor's operation. A related study appeared in Physics Essays , extending the analysis to the electromotive aspects of the device and the question of a nonzero electric field arising from a direct current in a stationary conductor.
His work follows a line of investigation into the Marinov Motor pursued by researchers such as Thomas Phipps and J. P. Wesley, who argue that the device poses difficulties for standard electrodynamics. These positions lie outside the physics mainstream.

David Jonsson
Known for Holographic model of consciousness and reality
David Jonsson is an author known for writing on a "holographic universe" interpretation of reality and consciousness. He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Ideas
Jonsson is the author of the book Holographic Universe: Law of Attraction & Money (2013), in which he argues that the visible world is a hologram generated by the observer. In his framing, the "real object" is a person's inner thoughts, while the outer, visible world is a reconstructed interference pattern created by the mind. These ideas fall outside the scientific mainstream and are presented by the author in a self-help and metaphysical register rather than as peer-reviewed physics.
He is also associated with fringe "new energy" material on the electromagnetism of fluid flow and temperature gradients, distributed through online alternative-physics archives.

Bergman's central claim was that the elementary particles are not dimensionless points with unexplained intrinsic properties, but real physical objects with real geometry — specifically, charge distributed on a thin spinning ring. In a 1990 paper in Galilean Electrodynamics with J. Paul Wesley, he showed that such a ring, with only four free parameters, reproduces the electron's mass, charge, spin, and magnetic moment; is stable under electromagnetic forces alone with no ad hoc binding assumption; does not radiate; explains the gyromagnetic ratio of 2 rather than postulating it; and yields the anomalous magnetic moment to higher order in agreement with measurement.
With Charles W. Lucas, Jr. , Thomas G. Barnes and Glen C. Collins , Bergman built this into a broader program covering the proton, neutron, nuclear structure, inertia, gravitation and molecular structure, published in the quarterly journal Foundations of Science which he edited (the Common Sense Science quarterly, not the Springer journal of the same name). David Lackey resides in Merrimack, New Hampshire. He conducts independent research in theoretical physics outside of the mainstream academic framework.

David M. Bower
Known for Critique of Einstein's special relativity; absolute space; Neo-Newtonian mechanics and electromagnetism (with Dennis P Allen )
Scientific career
Fields Physics , Relativity , Electrodynamics
David M. Bower is an independent researcher and critic of Einstein's special relativity who works within the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society community. He argues that the Lorentz–Poincaré (aether) version of relativity, with its preferred reference frame, is preferable to Einstein's version, and that space is absolute rather than purely relational. In recent years he has collaborated with Dennis P Allen on applying Allen's Neo-Newtonian mechanics to electromagnetism and to models of the elementary particles.
Biography
Little biographical detail about David M. Bower is publicly available; he publishes as an independent researcher without a listed institutional affiliation. His work has appeared as preprints on viXra since 2023, and he has presented in the CNPS online livestream series since October 2023, both alone and jointly with Dennis P. Allen.
Scientific contributions
The absolute nature of space
In A Simple Proof of the Absolute Nature of Space (2023), Bower offers what he describes as a logical extension and extrapolation of Newton's rotating-bucket argument. Where Newton used the curved surface of water in a spinning bucket to argue that rotation is absolute rather than merely relative, Bower extends the reasoning to argue that space possesses absolute properties with respect to translational motion as well as rotational motion. This conclusion places him in the classical, pre-Einsteinian tradition of absolute space, and underpins the rest of his critique of relativity.
Critique of Einstein's special relativity
Bower distinguishes sharply between two versions of special relativity: the Einsteinian version (which he abbreviates ESR), in which no reference frame is preferred, and the Lorentz aether theory (LAT/LET) developed chiefly by Lore

David Rosignoli (born 1972) is an American electrical engineer, a licensed professional engineer with more than fourteen years' practice as of 2011, and an experimentalist with an interest in anomalous and unconventional science and technology. He is Director of the Research Advisory Group for the Tesla Science Foundation, a member of the NTIC, and assistant organiser of the Tesla Conference.
Work
Rosignoli's contribution catalogued here is experimental rather than theoretical, which distinguishes it from most of this collection. Experimental Results in Measuring Atmospheric Electricity (2011), written with Michael R Treat and presented at the 18th Natural Philosophy Alliance conference, reports a measurement of the current drawable from the fair-weather atmospheric electric field. A metallised foil balloon lofted a 300-foot carbon-fibre tether, and a Keithley picoammeter isolated behind a remotely operated contactor recorded 0.8 μA at 275 feet — consistent with the roughly 1 μA that C. L. Stong had reported at 300 feet in Scientific American in 1974.
The paper is careful about method: the tether was kept off the ground on a varnished platform, the meter ran from a battery through an inverter, and readings were taken with the experimenters clear of the apparatus. Its practical findings — that an uninsulated carbon-fibre tether performs as well as the insulated wire earlier workers used, and that the splayed five-micron filaments of an uncoated tow make an efficient, very light collector — are of use to anyone repeating the measurement.

David S. Walton
Alma mater University of Newcastle
Known for Ivor Catt
Scientific career
Fields Atomic physics, electromagnetic theory, digital electronics
David S Walton is a British physicist, electronics engineer and teacher, known chiefly as a long-time collaborator of the British electronics engineer Ivor Catt . With Catt and Malcolm Davidson he formed the "Catt, Walton and Davidson" partnership, whose late-1970s articles and books challenged the conventional textbook treatment of Maxwell's displacement current and put forward a model of the capacitor as a transmission line.
Biography
Walton took his first degree in Physics at the University of Newcastle and remained there to carry out research in experimental atomic physics, leading to a PhD. His first teaching post was as a Lecturer in Physics at Trinity College Dublin, where he worked under the Nobel Prize winner E. T. S. Walton (no relation). At Trinity College he carried out research in electron time-of-flight spectroscopy and on anthracene scintillators.
He then left academic life to set up an electronics company, where he researched and published articles and a book on signal transmission and design issues in fast digital systems. This work led him on to the foundational concepts of electromagnetic theory. He subsequently worked for a multinational company and for a number of smaller companies, eventually running his own consultancy business in information technology; from 1999 to 2002 he was contracted to companies in Utrecht and Brussels to provide consultancy support for the management of their IT infrastructure.
In 2003 Walton made a complete career change and took up a physics teaching post at Emmanuel College, Gateshead, where he formally qualified as a teacher under the Graduate Teacher Programme. He taught at Emmanuel College for eight years before being appointed Head of Physics at Barnard Castle School in 2011.

Education

Talbott as editor, he revived the student magazine Pensée . Late in 1971 the brothers decided to devote a feature issue to Velikovsky's ideas; the response was so great that it grew, between 1972 and 1974, into a landmark ten-issue series titled Immanuel Velikovsky Reconsidered , reaching a circulation of between 10,000 and 20,000 subscribers and bringing renewed scholarly attention to Velikovsky's work.

David W. Thomson III (born 1960) is an American independent researcher, the discoverer and principal theoretician of the Aether Physics Model (APM), which he developed with James D. Bourassa . He is Science Director of the Quantum AetherDynamics Institute, the non-profit organization the two founded to develop the theory.
Aether Physics Model
Thomson says he arrived at the Aether Physics Model in February 2002, and in 2004 he and Bourassa incorporated the Quantum AetherDynamics Institute to develop it. The model treats space as permeated by a real, discrete medium — the aether — built from fundamental "aether units," each conceived as a quantum of rotating magnetic field, from which the properties of subatomic particles and the forces between them are held to follow.
Thomson presents the APM as an "improved quantum paradigm": where conventional physics, in his framing, describes what the universe does , the Aether Physics Model sets out to quantify what the universe is , deriving a unified force theory, an account of dark matter, and a claimed means of quantifying consciousness from a single quantized aether. He worked the approach out with Bourassa in the papers " A New Foundation for Physics " (2006) and " Electron Binding Energies in the Aether Physics Model " (2007), and in their book Secrets of the Aether (2004). The model is offered as a mathematically self-consistent alternative to the Standard Model rather than a modification of it, and is not accepted by mainstream physics.

David Wilcock (born 1973) is an American author, lecturer and media personality known for his writings on consciousness, ancient civilizations and an "aether"-based view of physics and cosmology. He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Ideas
Wilcock proposes that physical matter is formed by what he calls an "aether" or "Source Field" — an invisible, conscious, fluid-like source of universal energy. Drawing on the work of the Soviet astrophysicist Nikolai Kozyrev, he argues that rotation and its direction can produce anti-gravity and related effects, and that mainstream science has overlooked evidence for a conscious, energetic substrate underlying matter. These claims lie outside the accepted framework of modern physics and are not supported by the mainstream scientific community.
Wilcock develops these themes in books including The Source Field Investigations (2011) and The Synchronicity Key (2013), and through his website Divine Cosmos, where he publishes essays and lectures on "soul growth, ascension, and the evolution of consciousness." He has also appeared as a commentator in popular paranormal and "ancient aliens" media.

Dayton Clarence Miller (13 March 1866 – 22 February 1941) was an American physicist, astronomer and acoustician who spent more than three decades measuring the drift of the Earth through the ether , and who reported — consistently, and to the end of his life — that he had found it.
Miller occupies an unusual position in the literature collected on this wiki. He was not a dissident. He was as established as a physicist of his era could be: head of physics at the Case School of Applied Science for forty-three years, a member of the National Academy of Sciences, and president of the American Physical Society , in which capacity he delivered the 1926 address announcing his result. He worked with Edward Morley , co-author of the experiment his own work extended.
He matters here because his data did not go away . A large, careful, decades-long body of measurement, produced by a respected experimentalist using the most sensitive apparatus of its day, reported a small but systematic effect that the theory adopted in his lifetime says should not exist. That result was set aside rather than refuted — and much of the research documented on this wiki begins by going back to it. See Michelson–Morley experiment and Preferred frame .

Abstract
The geometrical interpretation of gravitation in general theory of relativity imparts certain mystical properties to the spacetime continuum. Abstract
In several recent papers we showed that choosing new sets of postulates, including classical (pre-Einstein) physics laws, within the main body of Einstein's special relativity theory (SRT) and applying the relativity principle, enables us to cancel the Lorentz transformation from the main body of SRT. In the present paper, and by following the same approach, we derive Einstein's equation E = mc 2 from classical physical laws such as the Lorentz force law and Newton's second law Einstein's equation is obtained without the usual approaches of thought experiment, conservation laws, considering collisions and also without the usual postulates of special relativity.
In this paper we also identify a fundamental conceptual flaw that has persisted for the past 100 years. The flaw is interpreting the formula E = mc 2 as the equivalence between inertial mass and any type of energy and in all contexts. It is shown in several recent papers that this is incorrect, that this is a misinterpretation. What Einstein considered to be a central consequence of special relativity is in fact derivable from (pre-Einstein) classical considerations. E = mc 2 becomes secondary, not fundamental, and whilst no doubt useful in certain circumstances, need not be valid in all generality.

Overview
Dated 24 February 1999 and never published in a journal, this three-page report by Morton F Spears offers a single mechanism for three cosmological puzzles then in the news: a universe apparently younger than its oldest stars, an expansion that appeared to be accelerating, and the missing mass called dark matter . Long ago, when everything was closer together, such a measurement would have returned a larger capacitance. Hence "perceived permittivity in the space of our Universe is decreasing with time and distance from the big bang origin."

Title Did the Universe have a Beginning?

Author(s) Tom Van Flandern

Volume 3

Read the full paper here (archived copy — the original link is no longer available)
Abstract
The big bang theory postulates that the entire universe originated in a cosmic explosion about 15 billion years ago. Such an idea had no serious constituency until Edwin Hubble discovered the redshift of galaxy light in the 1920s, which seemed to imply an expanding universe. However, our ability to test cosmological theories has vastly improved with modern telescopes covering all wavelengths, some of them in orbit. Despite the widespread acceptance of the big bang theory as a working model for interpreting new findings, not a single important prediction of the theory has yet been confirmed, and substantial evidence has accumulated against it. Here, we examine the evidence for the most fundamental postulate of the big bang, the expansion of the universe. We conclude that the evidence does not support the theory; and that it is time to stop patching up the theory to keep it viable, and to consider fundamentally new working models for the origin and nature of the universe in better agreement with the observations.

The Dinu Effect is the observation that two cylinders rotating under water attract or repel one another in exactly the pattern of two permanent magnets — attracting when spun in opposite directions and repelling when spun in the same direction — with no magnet, charge or field involved anywhere in the apparatus.
The effect is named after the Romanian physicist Ionel Dinu , who performed and filmed the underwater experiments from 2006 onward as part of a programme to show that electric, magnetic and gravitational forces are fluid-mechanical effects in a liquid aether . The name "Dinu Effect" was coined by David de Hilster in Principia Mathematica 2 , written with his father Robert de Hilster , where the effect is adopted as the experimental basis for the magnetic component of the Four Universal Motions .
Its importance to the researchers who use it is that it is a physical demonstration, not an argument . Magnetic-looking attraction and repulsion are produced in a bucket of water, in front of a camera, by rotation alone.
The experiment
The apparatus is deliberately simple. Two cylinders — in other runs, disks — are suspended in water and set rotating, and their subsequent motion is observed. The variable is the relative direction of rotation.
Opposite directions of rotation → the cylinders attract and move together.
Same direction of rotation → the cylinders repel and move apart.
This is the same rule that governs magnets, and it is the whole of the observation. Dinu has also run the experiment with rotating disks and has supported the physical work with computational fluid dynamics simulations.

Together with collaborators (notably V. A. Andreev), Tsipenyuk proposes an Extended Space Model (ESM) that enlarges the (1+3)-dimensional Minkowski spacetime of special relativity to a (1+4)-dimensional space, adding the interval S as a fifth coordinate. In this framework he argues that scalar gravity and electromagnetism can be unified into a single field, that particle rest masses need not be constant, and that a photon can carry a nonzero variable mass. This unification programme and its experimental interpretation lie outside the accepted framework of general relativity and the Standard Model.

Title Does the Sun Orbit a Dark Star?
Author(s) Glen W Deen
Keywords precession of the equinoxes, attractor
Published 2006
Journal Proceedings of the NPA
Volume 3
Number 1
Pages 14-23
Abstract
The precession of the equinoxes was discovered in the second century BC by Hipparchus, and it was described as a slow revolution of the whole field of stars about the ecliptic poles. This could be explained if the Sun orbited some unseen object. The modern explanation was given by Newton as being the slow rotation of the Earth's polar axis about the ecliptic poles caused by gravitational forces from the Sun and Moon on the non-uniform mass distribution in the oblate Earth. In the first model, the Earth's celestial equator is fixed in space, and the celestial sphere appears to rotate. In the modern model, the celestial sphere is fixed, and the celestial equator rotates. These two models are indistinguishable by astronomical observations. This paper computes a range of possible solar orbits, depending only on the assumed mass of the unseen attractor, that were obtained by minimizing the squared error in the ecliptic longitude of Regulus as measured by Hipparchus circa 128 BC, Ptolemy in 138 AD, 11 observations by Arabic astronomers in the period of A.D. 830-975, the modern longitude of Regulus, and the modern precession rate. An intriguing possibility is that many transneptunian objects and long-period comets may orbit the same attractor that the Sun orbits. Pluto could have been captured by the Sun, if it had been deflected by Neptune. The goal of this line of research is to see if there is a particular attractor mass that will cause Pluto to have been captured by the Sun.

Work
Roth's best-known experiment used a suspended magnetic torsion beam, essentially a bar magnet hung from a string and balanced at its center. When a strong magnet was placed on a nearby table with one pole directed toward the beam, the beam eventually settled toward the opposite pole after a series of oscillations. Roth reported that, after the arrangement had been maintained for about five days, the magnet could be moved a considerable distance away and the beam would still be attracted as though the magnet remained in place.
Roth interpreted this apparent "magnetic memory" as evidence that magnetism is a flow within the aether: once such a flow is established in a localized region of space, he argued, it can persist there even after the magnet that produced it is removed. Abstract
The theory of the object known in general relativity as a Black Hole is not fully worked out and remains a source of various controversies. This paper shows that true black holes do not exist in nature due to forces that prevent the formation of singularities and event horizons. A reconstruction of the derivation of the Einstein field equations of general relativity shows that a force causes a phase-change transition from matter to energy near the Planck scale. This phase-change is the cause of an ejection process from the nuclear region of galaxies and ultimately results in the formation of gas, dust, stars, and other structures throughout the Universe.
Overview
Presented at the Natural Philosophy Alliance conference at Storrs, Connecticut in 2009, this is a long synthesis paper — roughly forty printed pages, much of it consisting of extended verbatim quotation from other authors, which Westergard assembles into a single argument. His own contribution is the closing third: the dynamics of what he renames "Degenerate Hydrogen Wells," and the account of cosmic structure formation that follows from them.
The claim is that the black hole of general relativity is an artifact rather than an object. Gravitational collapse, on this view, does not run to a singularity; it stops at a definite limit where matter undergoes a phase change into pure spin, and the stored angular momentum is eventually ejected — supplying the gas, dust, stars and galaxies of a steady-state, non-expanding universe. Author(s) David Tombe

Published 2007
Journal General Science Journal

Abstract
An abominable by-product of the modern relativity era is the widely circulated notion that a magnetic field is the relativistic component of the electric field. This idea arises out of applying the Lorentz transformation to Heaviside's versions of Maxwell's equations. The result yields both the Biot-Savart law and the Lorentz force along with the relativistic conversion factors. This article aims to demonstrate that the Lorentz transformation of the Maxwell/Heaviside equations, as regards producing the vxB component of the Lorentz force, is merely doing what a Galilean transformation would also do. It is restoring the convective component that was part of Maxwell's original fourth equation, and which Heaviside and Gibbs took away in 1884. This article also demonstrates that the Biot-Savart law is a solution to Maxwell's equations independently of the Lorentz transformation.
Overview
E = v×B and Maxwell's Fourth Equation is a five-page paper by David Tombe , dated 30 April 2007 and published in the General Science Journal . It argues against the idea that the magnetic field is a relativistic by-product of the electric field, and in favour of the view that the v×B term was part of Maxwell's original equations until Heaviside and Gibbs removed it.
The historical claim comes first. "It is a virtually unknown fact in physics circles that the expression that bears the misnomer ‘the Lorentz force’ is actually equation (D) of the original set of eight ‘Maxwell's Equations’. The Lorentz force existed when Lorentz was a young boy." Tombe writes it in modern form as
E = −grad ψ − ∂A/∂t + v×B
and notes that it also appears as equation (77) of Maxwell's 1861 On Physical Lines of Force .

Edward Arthur Milne (14 February 1896 – 21 September 1950) was a British astrophysicist and mathematician, Rouse Ball Professor of Mathematics at Oxford from 1928, who built a complete cosmology out of the special theory of relativity and a symmetry postulate, without using general relativity or curved space at all. He named that postulate the cosmological principle .
Milne's first career was in stellar physics. He worked out the theory of radiative transfer in stellar atmospheres, the Milne–Eddington approximation for line formation, the theory of the outer layers of stars, and the escape of atoms from stellar surfaces. He disagreed sharply with Eddington over the internal constitution of stars, arguing for degenerate cores against Eddington's standard model. He was awarded the Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society in 1935 and was its President from 1943 to 1945.
Kinematic relativity
From 1932 Milne turned to cosmology. His starting point was that the general theory of relativity smuggles in far more structure than the evidence warrants, and that a cosmology should be deduced from as little as possible. He assumed only special relativity, a set of equivalent fundamental observers, and the requirement that the universe look the same to all of them — his cosmological principle.

Keywords gravitational potential, earth
Published 2011
Journal Proceedings of the NPA
Volume 8
No. of pages 4

Abstract
In the study of an Earth orbiting satellite, the terms of the series expansion of the Earth's gravitational potential can be expressed as functions of the eccentricity of the satellite. These functions are also known as eccentricity functions. The series expansion of these functions given by Kaula [2] appears to result in instabilities at high eccentricities. When calculating the eccentricity functions, researchers resort to numerical integration techniques instead. The approach followed in this contribution bypasses the problem of instability at high eccentricities by using a Hansen coefficient definition. As a test, we first calculate analytical expressions for various known eccentricity functions and then we proceed with the calculation of the eccentricity functions associated with degree and order 20, 30, 40, 50 sectorial harmonic coefficient expansion of the gravitational potential. Our calculation demonstrates the efficiency of Hansen coefficient approach that differs from that given by Kaula. It is efficient, fast, and can easily be performed with the help of a personal computer, with no instabilities at higher eccentricities.
Overview
Ioannis Haranas, Omiros Ragos and Michael Harney address a computational problem in satellite geodesy: how to evaluate the eccentricity functions that appear in the spherical harmonic expansion of a planet's gravitational potential, without the numerical instabilities that afflict the standard series.

Edmund Storms obtained a Ph.D. in radiochemistry from Washington University (St. Louis) and is retired from the Los Alamos National Laboratory after thirty-four years of service. His work there involved basic research in the field of high temperature chemistry as applied to materials used in nuclear power and propulsion reactors, including studies of the "cold fusion" effect. Over seventy reviewed publications and monographs resulted from this work as well as several books, all describing an assortment of material properties. He presently lives in Santa Fe where he is investigating the "cold fusion" effect in his own laboratory. These studies have resulted in sixteen presentations to various conferences including the ACS and APS. In addition, twenty-one papers have been published including three complete scientific reviews of the field, one published in 1991, another in 1996 and the latest one in 1998. A critical evaluation of the Pons-Fleichmann Effect was published in 2000. In May 1993, he was invited to testify before a congressional committee about the "cold fusion" effect. In 1998, Wired magazine honored him as one of 25 people who are making significant contributions to new ideas.
Work on cold fusion
Storms is among the small number of researchers with an established mainstream career in nuclear science who continued working on the cold fusion claim after most laboratories abandoned it in the early 1990s. His approach has been that of a materials chemist rather than a physicist: he has argued consistently that the phenomenon's notorious irreproducibility is not evidence against it but the central clue to its nature, and that the reaction cannot occur in ordinary metal but only at some rare structure formed by chance during preparation — a condition he named the nuclear-active-environment , or NAE.

Eduard Krausz is a German diploma engineer (Dipl.-Ing.) and independent researcher based in Groß-Umstadt, known for an alternative theory of gravity in which gravitation is the effect of a physical medium rather than a property of mass. He set out his ideas in the 1998 book Das Universum funktioniert anders - Realität kontra Relativität .
Scientific work
Krausz rejects the standard account in which gravity is an unchanging quantity fixed by an object's mass. In his Alternative Gravitation Theory he treats gravity instead as the action of an aether — a medium he pictures as a pressure wave issuing from space that pushes bodies toward a planet and toward one another. On his account a fluid flows around and permeates all bodies and particles in proportion to their mass, and he holds that this picture accounts for nuclear- and astro-physical phenomena more consistently than mainstream physics, which he regards as too narrowly fixed on particles.
In 1991, at the Fachhochschule Gelsenkirchen, Krausz carried out an experiment — since known as the Gelsenkirchen experiment — which he presented as evidence that gravity can be partially shielded. The experiment was reported in the German magazine Raum & Zeit and was later the subject of an independent replication attempt. His work has circulated in the German-language critical-physics and alternative-science communities rather than in the mainstream literature, and his conclusions are not accepted by mainstream physics.

Edward Henry Dowdye, Jr. (13 November 1943 – 31 December 2020) was an American laser optics physicist, retired from NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, and the author of the Extinction Shift Principle — a purely classical emission theory offered as an alternative to both special and general relativity.
Dowdye was unusual in this literature on two counts. First, his objection to general relativity was observational rather than philosophical : he argued that light bending near the Sun occurs only at the thin plasma rim and not in the vacuum beyond it, which is what refraction predicts and not what gravitation predicts, and he pursued this claim through the published deflection and timing data. Second, he was by his own description the only working emission theorist of his generation — the tradition having lapsed since Walter Ritz (1878–1909) — and his version was distinctive in applying to gravitation as well as electromagnetism, where earlier emission theories addressed light alone.
He was one of the featured scientists in the feature-length documentary Einstein Wrong - The Miracle Year (2013), in which he appears alongside Patricia Anne de Hilster , Robert de Hilster and David de Hilster .

Edward Williams Morley (29 January 1838 – 24 February 1923) was an American chemist whose name is attached to the most argued-over experiment in modern physics, but whose own reputation in his lifetime rested on something else: he was the most exact analytical chemist of his generation.
Life and chemical work
Morley was born in Newark, New Jersey, the son of a Congregational minister, and was taught at home before entering Williams College. He trained for the ministry at Andover Theological Seminary and was ordained, but was unable to secure a pulpit; in 1869 he took a professorship of chemistry and natural history at Western Reserve College in Hudson, Ohio, moving with the college to Cleveland in 1882. He remained there until his retirement in 1906.
His major chemical work was the determination of the atomic weight of oxygen relative to hydrogen, published in 1895 after more than a decade of work in which he prepared both gases to a purity nobody had previously achieved and weighed the water formed by their combination. The result stood as the standard value for years and is still cited as a model of precision measurement. He also carried out careful studies of the oxygen content of the atmosphere, and served as president of the American Chemical Society in 1899. He was awarded the Davy Medal of the Royal Society in 1907 and the Elliott Cresson Medal in 1912.

Edwin Eugene Klingman is an American physicist and author known for his work on a self-interacting gravitomagnetic "C-field" and for a long series of essays submitted to the Foundational Questions Institute (FQXi). He is listed in The Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Background
Klingman earned a PhD in physics and worked as a research physicist in atomic and molecular physics. His doctoral work was later published as The Automatic Theory of Physics , which describes how a robot might derive a theory of physics from pattern recognition and entropy.
Ideas
Klingman argues for a gravitomagnetic field, which he calls the "C-field," treated as a continuous field filling space everywhere. He proposes that the C-field associated with massive rotating black holes offers a simpler account of the light-years-long astrophysical jets than magnetic-field explanations. In his FQXi essays he also questions foundational assumptions of quantum mechanics, including aspects of Bell's theorem, and explores the nature of time, information and consciousness. These positions lie outside the accepted mainstream of physics.

Edwin Powell Hubble (November 20, 1889 – September 28, 1953) was an American astronomer who established that the spiral nebulae are galaxies far beyond the Milky Way, and who discovered in 1929 the linear relation between a galaxy's redshift and its distance now known as Hubble's law .
His name is attached to the expanding universe, and his relation is universally cited as its observational proof. This is one of the more striking ironies in the history of cosmology, because Hubble himself never accepted that interpretation , warned repeatedly against it, and in later life inclined toward a static, endless universe in which redshift arises from some unrecognised principle of nature. His caution is regularly invoked by the researchers catalogued on this wiki.
Early life and education
Hubble was born in Marshfield, Missouri, in 1889. He studied mathematics and astronomy at the University of Chicago and then went to Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar, where he read law at his father's urging. He passed the bar and practised briefly in Louisville, Kentucky, before abandoning law for astronomy — returning to Chicago for his doctorate and joining the staff of Mount Wilson Observatory.
Galaxies beyond the Milky Way
Using the 100-inch telescope at Mount Wilson, then the largest in the world, Hubble identified Cepheid variable stars in the Andromeda Nebula in 1924. Because the period–luminosity relation of Cepheids allows their distance to be calculated, he could show that Andromeda lies far outside the Milky Way. Efficiency is a four-page article by Leslee A Kulba , published in 2010 in issue 48 of the Electric Spacecraft Journal , the journal's final double issue. It is the fourth part of the ten-part handbook on perpetual motion and its testing that Kulba, the journal's technical editor, contributed to that issue, and it follows immediately on " Conservation Laws ".
The text of the article has not been recoverable, and this page describes its subject and its place in the series rather than its argument.
The subject
Efficiency is the ratio of useful output to total input, and the reason it earns four pages here — more than the conservation laws themselves — is that the ratio is much easier to get wrong than it looks. An over-unity claim is a claim that this number exceeds one. Most of the ways it can exceed one have nothing to do with new physics.
Efficiency is not coefficient of performance
The commonest confusion in the whole subject is between efficiency and coefficient of performance . A domestic heat pump delivers three or four joules of heat into a house for every joule of electricity it consumes, and its COP is therefore 3 or 4. This is not a violation of anything: the extra energy is not created but moved , pumped from the cold outside air into the warm inside, and the electricity pays only for the pumping. A device whose output is of a different kind from its input — heat moved versus work supplied — can have a ratio above one all day long.
Several claimed over-unity devices are of exactly this character, drawing on an unmeasured ambient reservoir. Abstract
Einstein postulated in his 1905 article that light speed is isotropic in all inertial frames in order to derive the Lorentz Transformations. But the light speed postulate is logically wrong for the following reason: suppose, a short light pulse is emitted from a source mounted, say, in the origin of the coordinate system K, which is at rest. A coordinate system K' is moving at v in the x -direction. At the moment, when the origins of both K and K' are coinciding, one spherical wave front is lounged at the origin of K. This means that there will be one spherical wave-front expanding around the origin of K, because the origin of K' moves away at v . But the Lorentz Transformations transform this pulse (lounged in K) into a wave-front spherically expanding in K', although there cannot be such a spherically expanding wave-front around the origin of K'. How could there be one, as only one spherically expanding wave-front was generated around the origin of K, where the emitter is mounted! K' moves away at v , without carrying with it a spherically expanding wave front at the origin of K'. But the Lorentz transformation equations are predicting that! This cannot be correct! It is logically impossible!

There is strong evidence that the forces of nature are caused by elastic strings. When nuclear physicists separate quarks, a strong force of attraction develops between them and the greater the separation the greater the force pulling them back together. The gluons that bind quarks behave like elastic strings. Stars in the Milky Way Galaxy appear to rotate far too fast for the stars to remain in orbit; however, their rotation can be explained if gravitons are elastic strings that gain greater potential energy when they act across great distances. Gravitons, like gluons, have the characteristics of elastic strings. This same finding explains why electrons remain in orbit about the nucleus of the atom even though their velocities appear far too fast for them to stay in orbit. Protons and electrons behave as though they are connected by elastic strings. This also explains rubber bands and steel springs that gain potential energy when stretched. Elastic strings can be used to explain all the forces of nature and a myriad of other conundrums of science.

Kelland David Terry proposes that every force in nature is transmitted by physical strings possessing what he calls perfect elasticity and perfect cohesion — a framework he names VES theory, for Virtual Elastic String. His starting observation is that quark confinement already looks like this: separate two quarks and the attraction between them grows rather than falling off, exactly as a stretched rubber band pulls harder the further it is drawn. Gluons, he concludes, behave like elastic strings.

content_preview:
Entropy is a measure of the number of microscopic arrangements consistent with a system's macroscopic state, and equivalently a measure of the energy in a system that is unavailable to do work.
The standard account
The concept arose from the study of heat engines. Rudolf Clausius introduced the term in 1865, defining the change in entropy of a system as the heat exchanged reversibly divided by the absolute temperature, and stating the second law of Thermodynamics in the form that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases. Ludwig Boltzmann then gave the statistical interpretation, S = k log W , where W counts the microstates compatible with the observed macrostate; the constant k now carries his name and, since the 2019 revision of the SI, has the exact defined value 1.380649 × 10 −23 J/K. Shannon's 1948 measure of information has the same mathematical form, and the connection between the two is more than formal.
Two consequences drive most of the argument about entropy. The first is the arrow of time : the microscopic laws of physics are very nearly time-symmetric, yet entropy increase picks out a direction. The usual account traces this not to the dynamics but to the initial condition — the universe began in a state of extraordinarily low entropy, and everything since has been relaxation from it. Why it did so is an acknowledged open problem, not a settled one. The second is the heat death argument, made by Helmholtz, Kelvin and Clausius in the mid-nineteenth century: if the universe is a finite isolated system, its entropy must rise to a maximum, after which no further work can be extracted.
On this wiki
The heat-death extrapolation is where researchers here concentrate their objection, and the objection is usually about the isolated system premise rather than about thermodynamics itself.

Why decay lowers entropy
The mechanism is the one that runs through the whole theory. Carezani then narrows what the law governs. "It is important to realize that the entropy principle refers exclusively to heat, that is, caloric energy." Eppur Si Muove (Italian for "and yet it moves," the phrase traditionally attributed to Galileo) is a book by the Bulgarian dissident physicist Stefan Marinov (1931–1997), first published in 1977 and reissued in a fourth edition in 2008. It gathers Marinov's experimental and theoretical case against Albert Einstein's special theory of relativity , centred on his claim to have measured the absolute velocity of the Earth through the aether by detecting a direction-dependence in the one-way speed of light .
The book
The core of Eppur Si Muove is Marinov's account of the experiments he devised to detect the Earth's motion relative to absolute space. Chief among them is his "coupled-shutters" (later "coupled-mirrors") method, in which two rotating shutters or mirrors mounted on a common shaft are used to compare the time of flight of light travelling in opposite directions along the same axis. Marinov reported that this arrangement revealed an anisotropy in the observed one-way velocity of light, from which he calculated an absolute velocity of the Earth of roughly 360 km/s in a definite direction — a result he presented as a direct measurement of motion through the aether and as a refutation of the relativistic postulate that the one-way speed of light is the same in every frame.
Alongside the experiments, the book sets out Marinov's own "absolute space–time" theory: a reworking of relativistic mechanics and electrodynamics in which the world-invariant constancy of the two-way velocity of light is retained, but absolute simultaneity and a preferred rest frame — the aether — are restored. The fourth edition carries a preface by the Soviet physicist Andrei D. Sakharov and a detailed description of the apparatus, together with Marinov's replies to his critics.

The paper presents the correspondence between physical quantities used in electrodynamics on the one hand and on the other those applied in elasticity and hydrodynamics having taken into account the SI units of physical quantities and assumed an analogy between mass and electric charge. Due to such correspondence almost every equation of electrodynamics is accompanied by an equation used in theory of elastic waves or hydrodynamics. Some changes concerning the form or the understanding of several equations are proposed. It has been shown that the Coulomb gauge and the first Helmholtz equation used in hydrodynamics have exactly the same physical meaning. Lorentz gauge with its sign changed is recognized as corresponding to one of the relations between stress and strain used in the theory of pressure elastic waves. The formula for the energy volume density of electromagnetic waves was modified in order to obtain the consistency with the corresponding formula for elastic S waves. Then the formula for the volume density of elastic force corresponding to that of the Lorentz force is proposed. The equivalence principle is the statement that the mass which resists acceleration (inertial mass) and the mass which responds to gravity (gravitational mass) are the same thing, so that all bodies fall alike in a gravitational field and a uniformly accelerated laboratory cannot be distinguished locally from one at rest in a gravitational field.
The standard account
The observation that bodies of different weight fall at the same rate goes back to Galileo, and Newton tested it with pendulums of different composition in the Principia . The empirical statement — that the ratio of gravitational to inertial mass is the same for all substances — is called the weak equivalence principle or the universality of free fall. It was tested to high precision by Loránd Eötvös with a torsion balance from 1889 onwards, and the Eötvös–Pekár–Fekete experiments published in 1922 remain a reference point in the literature. Modern torsion-balance work and lunar laser ranging constrain the Eötvös parameter to roughly one part in 10 13 , and the French MICROSCOPE satellite mission (2016–2018, final analysis 2022) tightened this to about one part in 10 15 for titanium and platinum test masses. No violation has been detected.
Einstein took a further step in 1907, in what he later called the happiest thought of his life: he proposed that a freely falling observer feels no gravity at all, and that all local physics — not just falling bodies — is the same in a freely falling frame as in an inertial frame far from any mass. This stronger statement, usually called the Einstein equivalence principle , adds local Lorentz invariance and local position invariance to the universality of free fall, and it is the foundation on which General Relativity is built: gravity is geometrised precisely because it can be locally transformed away. Mach held chairs at Graz, Prague and finally Vienna, where his professorship was in the history and theory of the inductive sciences. As an experimentalist he is remembered for the photographic study of supersonic projectiles — he and Peter Salcher published images of the shock cone in 1887, and the ratio of a body's speed to the speed of sound in the medium was later named the Mach number in his honour. He also did extensive work on the physiology of sensation, including the visual contrast effect known as Mach bands.
His lasting influence, however, is philosophical. Erwin Rudolf Josef Alexander Schrödinger (12 August 1887 – 4 January 1961) was an Austrian theoretical physicist who created wave mechanics in 1926 and shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Dirac . He is unusual among the founders of quantum theory in that he spent the rest of his life objecting to what the theory was taken to mean.
In a series of four papers in Annalen der Physik during 1926, Schrödinger took de Broglie 's matter waves seriously and wrote down the wave equation that carries his name, deriving the hydrogen spectrum from it as an eigenvalue problem. In the same year he proved that his wave mechanics and Heisenberg 's matrix mechanics are mathematically equivalent. He succeeded Planck at Berlin in 1927, left Germany in 1933 in protest at the Nazi regime, and after a period at Oxford and a dangerous year in Graz settled at the Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies from 1940 to 1956.
His 1944 book What Is Life? argued that the hereditary material must be an aperiodic crystal carrying a code-script, and is credited by Crick, Watson and Wilkins among others with drawing them into molecular biology. He also worked on unified field theory alongside Einstein , and wrote extensively on philosophy, including Nature and the Greeks , Mind and Matter and My View of the World — the last drawing openly on Vedanta.
