Abstract
The second of two papers arguing that the theory of moving charge carriers cannot explain the electrical conduction of the Hall effect . Part II attacks the concept of the positively charged "hole" as a category mistake, and proposes instead that the sign of the Hall coefficient is governed by crystal structure , within a model in which conduction is the propagation of a state of charge distribution rather than a flow of charges.
The argument against holes
Marinsek's target is the standard account in which conduction in a solid is carried by electrons and by holes — vacancies in a filled band treated as particles of effective positive charge. His objection is not quantitative but conceptual, and he states it as a category mistake : "a successive occurrence of different holes is not identical with the movement of one hole." A hole, on his account, is simply the previous location of an electron; a location cannot move unless the atom moves, which the theory does not claim.
He works this through the "row of seats" analogy used in textbook expositions and in the Wikipedia article on the electron hole, in which people shift one seat along and the empty seat appears to travel the other way. The analogy fails, he argues, on the same point: seat #4 does not move towards the edge of the row, and all that occurs is a succession of empty seats.
From this he draws the stronger claim, which is where the ontological objection lies. Treating the absence of an electron as a particle amounts to a transubstantiation of an empty place into a positron — a creation ex nihilo . title: The 1855 Weber-Kohlrausch Experiment (The Speed of Light)
content_preview:
Title The 1855 Weber-Kohlrausch Experiment (The Speed of Light)
Read in full Link to paper
Author(s) David Tombe
Published 2019
Journal General Science Journal
Abstract
In the year 1855, German physicists Wilhelm Eduard Weber and Rudolf Kohlrausch performed an experiment with a Leyden jar and established the ratio between electrostatic and electrodynamic units of charge. This ratio became known as Weber’s constant and it is numerically equal to c√2, where c is the speed of light. In 1857, another German physicist Gustav Robert Kirchhoff used Weber’s constant to conclude that electric signals travel along a wire at the speed of light. A few years later in 1861, Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell was working on the physical medium responsible for magnetic lines of force and he had established a linkage between its transverse elasticity and the ratio of electrostatic to electromagnetic units of charge. Electromagnetic units of charge are related to electrodynamic units by a factor of √2. In order to evaluate this ratio, Maxwell looked up Weber’s results, and on converting Weber’s constant into electromagnetic units, the speed of light was exposed. This paper sets out to establish the fundamental origins of the speed of light.
Overview
Dated 14 April 2019 and posted to the General Science Journal , this paper by David Tombe of Northern Ireland is a historical reconstruction with a thesis attached. Its subject is the experiment Wilhelm Weber and Rudolf Kohlrausch performed in 1855, which measured the ratio between the electrostatic and electrodynamic units of charge and so, unexpectedly, produced a velocity.
Tombe traces what followed: Kirchhoff's use of that ratio in 1857 to conclude that electric signals travel along a wire at the speed of light; and Maxwell's use of it in 1861, while working on the elastic medium responsible for magnetic lines of force, to expose the speed of light directly and connect it to the transverse elasticity of the luminiferous medium.

Overview

Its organising idea is the new event : an intervention in the time-reversible dynamical trajectories of particles, something "not predicted by those laws". Because the dynamical laws of physics run equally well in either time direction, Burns argues, once a trajectory is fixed by initial conditions it admits no later alteration; the only way a new event can enter is by changing the initial conditions themselves. Random quantum events, free will and psychokinesis (PK) are all treated as instances of the same formal category.

An asymptote is a goal that can probably never be reached, and if reached, cannot be crossed. If crossed, there may be no return. There are at least six asymptotes that apply to our universe. Robert Heaston's essay is a philosophical argument rather than a calculation — he says explicitly that "no mathematics or equations will be used." He identifies six such bounds and arranges them as the faces of a box. The pairing is deliberate: birth and death are limits on time, light speed and collapse are limits on space, absolute zero and the superforce are limits on matter, so that the box's structure follows from the three basic units.

The Atom is a 1920 book by Albert Cushing Crehore setting out an alternative to the Bohr model of the atom. It is not an exposition of accepted atomic physics but an argument against the theory that had just become standard, together with a rival theory of Crehore's own — one in which the hydrogen atom has two electrons rather than one, a whole series of spectral lines is emitted in a single operation rather than one line per jump, and gravitation is derived from the motion of the electrons inside atoms .
The book is the mathematical statement of a programme Crehore had described without equations three years earlier in The Mystery of Matter and Energy: Recent Progress as to the Structure of Matter (1917), and it was followed the same year by The New Physics .
Why the book was written
Crehore explains in the first pages that he would ordinarily have published this work as a series of papers in the technical journals, as he had done for many years, but that the argument needed more space than a journal would give and that condensing it would weaken rather than strengthen it. He is explicit about what he is doing:
It would be false modesty to try to disguise the fact that the subject of atomic theory is treated in a new form from the beginning to the end of the volume… This has made it necessary to emphasize the points where the current theory of the atom, that due to Dr. N. Bohr, is deficient.
He adds that Bohr's work is "most suggestive, and as marking an epoch in the progress of atomic theory." The dispute is with the theory, not with its author.

Summary
Having given a session on Lambda-CDM cosmology, Harry Ricker found he could not answer a simple question — what exactly is the cosmic microwave background? — and set out to trace it from the theory to the satellites. His conclusion is about the story rather than the physics: the standard account is constructed by hindsight, and the details do not fit it. Who actually predicted it
The textbooks say Gamow predicted the background and that Penzias and Wilson confirmed it by accident. Ricker went to the sources and found otherwise. Gamow's 1946 paper contains nothing about microwave background radiation; it postulates neutrons decaying into protons and electrons in a hot early state. Alpher and Herman's 1948 paper, which corrects Gamow, gives about 5 K — but for the remnant gas , not for any radiation.
The prediction Ricker credits comes from the Princeton group. Dicke's own account has the hot cosmology in disfavour — probably, Ricker thought, because it could not synthesise the heavier elements — and revived by Hoyle and Tayler's work on helium around 1962. What the Princeton group added, and what is now forgotten, is that their motivation was an oscillating universe: a closed universe contracting to a hot bounce and re-expanding, which avoids having to assume the energy of the universe at t = 0. Abstract
Astronomers use the Doppler-shifted absorption (dark) lines in the spectra of moving astronomic bodies to measure their radial velocities respect to Earth. A dark line, however, is the absence of radiation. How, then, can it be red-shifted or blue-shifted in any sense? This paper investigates this problem trying to comply with QM, and with both, the classical Doppler effect and its relativistic version. For relativity this is the problem: the Doppler-shifted dark lines are produced by absorption in the atmosphere of the selfsame star that emits the radiation. So it looks like a Doppler shift without relative motion. For QM the problem is how to harmonize the frequency shift with Planck's quantum relation, E=hf , where the frequency f is uniquely defined by a given energy level of a given atom in a stationary frame of reference. The Expanding Earth: Some Consequences of Dirac's Gravitation Hypothesis is a 1971 book by the physicist Pascual Jordan , published by Pergamon Press. It is an English translation (by Arthur Beer) of his 1966 German work Die Expansion der Erde (Braunschweig: Friedrich Vieweg).
Overview
Jordan takes up Paul Dirac's "large numbers" hypothesis of a gradual weakening of the gravitational constant G over cosmic time, and works out its geophysical consequences. He argues that, as gravity has weakened, the Earth has slowly expanded — swelling from an initial ball perhaps only about 7,000 km in diameter to its present size — and he connects this to continental drift, the growth of the ocean basins, and other geological evidence. The book is a rare instance of a major theoretical physicist developing the Expanding-Earth idea from a specific cosmological hypothesis.
About the author
Pascual Jordan (1902–1980) was a German theoretical physicist and one of the founders of quantum mechanics and quantum field theory (the Born–Heisenberg–Jordan "three-man paper," and Jordan–Wigner quantization). In his later career he worked on cosmology and gravitation, including scalar-tensor ("Jordan–Brans–Dicke") theories of varying gravity, of which the Expanding Earth was a proposed consequence.

The Farce of Physics is a book by Bryan G Wallace (1933–1997), copyright 1993, arguing that "modern theoretical physics has become to a large degree, little more than an elaborate farce." It is part memoir, part polemic and part sociology of science: an account of Wallace's roughly fifty-year career as a physicist working outside the academic mainstream, organised around his contention that Einstein's second postulate — the constancy of the velocity of light — is contradicted by interplanetary radar data and is the load-bearing assumption of everything built on it.
It was never issued by a publisher. Wallace circulated it over the early internet, and it remains freely readable in full; see Reading the book below.
The central argument
Wallace states the thesis of the book most compactly in Chapter 4, prompted by a reader's question in Marilyn vos Savant's newspaper column about what single discovery would overturn modern science:
Einstein's special relativity theory with his second postulate that the speed of light in space is constant is the linchpin that holds the whole range of modern physics theories together. Shatter this postulate, and modern physics becomes an elaborate farce!
His evidence for shattering it is the one he had pressed since 1969: that published interplanetary radar data, in particular the 1961 radar contact with Venus, fit a classical c + v relative velocity better than a constant c . The book's wider claim is that the physics community's failure to engage with this is not an accident but a symptom — of funding structures, of peer review, and of what he regards as physics having taken on the character of a faith.
The title is a deliberate echo of Fritjof Capra's The Tao of Physics , which Wallace quotes

Summary
James Arathoon began by disclaiming expertise. Why it matters
α = e 2 /4πε 0 ℏ c is the only dimensionless number that can be made from these constants of nature, all units cancelling. Its inverse is close to but not exactly 137.
Arathoon stressed something usually left out: the constant now sits at the heart of the SI system. Where once only the speed of light was fixed by definition, the Planck constant and the elementary charge are fixed too, so the metre follows from c , the kilogram from h and the ampere from e — and a measurement of α ties the system together. The permeability of free space, formerly defined as exactly 4π × 10 −7 , is now a measured quantity that happens to sit within the error bounds of that value.
The open questions he set out: whether α approximates a notional irrational number as π does; whether it can be computed by an algorithm independent of experiment; and whether it is constant through the history of the universe.

"The Holor Representation of Polarization" is a 1994 paper by Domina Eberle Spencer , Uma Y Shama and Terri L Mascardo , published in the Journal of the Illuminating Engineering Society . It applies the algebra of holors to the description of the polarization of light.
Overview
A holor is a mathematical object made up of one or more independent components (called merates ), introduced by Parry Moon and Domina Eberle Spencer in their book Theory of Holors (Cambridge University Press, 1986). The holor concept was proposed as a generalization broad enough to embrace scalars, vectors, matrices, tensors and other multi-component quantities within a single formalism, with a common index notation and a general account of how the components transform. The motivation is that many quantities useful in physics are not tensors, even though the tensor calculus is often treated as the only rigorous framework; holor algebra is offered as a way of handling that wider class of entities on the same footing.
In this paper the authors turn that framework on polarization — the orientation of the transverse oscillations of a light wave. Polarized light is conventionally described in several separate ways: by the two-component complex Jones vector, by the four real Stokes parameters, and by the Mueller matrices that transform them as light passes through optical elements. The paper recasts these descriptions within the holor formalism, giving a unified holor representation of the polarization state and of the operations that act on it. It belongs to a series of works in which Spencer and Moon extended holor methods into physical optics and photometry, the field in which much of their joint work appeared.

filename: The Mediums for Light are Hiding in Plain Sight.html
title: The Mediums for Light are Hiding in Plain Sight
content_preview:
Title The Mediums for Light are Hiding in Plain Sight
Author(s) Richard O Calkins
Keywords propagation of light
Published 2015
No. of pages 12
Abstract
The propagation of light remains one of the enduring mysteries of science. Unlike every other known kind of wave, it travels at a constant speed without a medium of propagation. What supports its travel in empty space? Why is its speed so constant? And why is it so very fast? Even Einstein gave up trying to puzzle it out and simply stated the propagation of light as a postulate. While Maxwell’s equations explain the behavior (the what) of light, they don’t explain the how. They show that the speed of light is determined by two constants - epsilon and mu - but not why these two constants have the values that they do rather than having some other values. So our questions remain: how and why? Maxwell’s equations actually do answer these questions. We just haven’t understood the message because of our human laundry list of implicit assumptions about the characteristics required of medium of propagation. As often happens with implicit assumptions, nearly all of them are wrong.
Light has not one but two mediums of propagation. The electric fields in electromagnetic waves are the medium of propagation for the magnetic fields, and the magnetic fields are the medium of propagation for the electric fields. Their dance with each other is what moves light through empty space, much like molecules of air do when propagating sound. Ironically, since the waves of light and the dancing electric and magnetic fields are the same things, the mediums of propagation quite literally have been hiding in plain sight.
This paper examines both the equation for the speed of sound and Maxwell’s equations from a new perspective. In essence, it performs a mathematical autopsy of both to illuminate what lies within and, in the process, solves the mysteries of light’s propagation as simply the laws of physics at work.

Einstein's 1915 calculation, which recovered the figure from general relativity without adjustable parameters, is generally regarded as the theory's first and cleanest empirical success.
Anyone proposing to remove general relativity from the account must therefore supply the 43 arcseconds from somewhere else. This is what the monograph attempts.

Roger J Anderton , who hosts most of the society's Saturday sessions, here gave the talk himself, continuing a series on the metaphysics underlying Einstein's relativity. The claim is structural rather than technical: the relativity principle is the foundation everything else is built on, and if the foundation is misstated then the building is unsound. He prepared the material in dialogue with ChatGPT and said so openly, explaining that the published literature says very little about Lorentz's ether theory in the detail he wants, and that of the assistants he has tried this one is the most willing to set out a case against the mainstream position rather than simply restating it.
What Einstein actually said
The starting text is the statement from the 1905 paper: the laws by which the states of physical systems undergo change are not affected whether these changes of state be referred to one or the other of two systems of coordinates in uniform translatory motion. In plain words, all physical laws are the same in any inertial frame and no experiment performed in uniform motion can reveal whether you are moving or at rest. Abstract
During 1908 and 1909 Ritz and Einstein battled of what we now call the time arrows of electrodynamics and entropy. Ritz argued that electrodynamic irreversibility was one of the roots of the second law of thermodynamics, while Einstein defended Maxwell-Lorentz electromagnetic time symmetry. Microscopic reversibility remains a cornerstone of our current paradigm, yet we are finding more and more evidence that experimentally discerned time arrows are asymmetrical and that they all point from past to future. This paper furnishes some comments about events leading up to the Ritz-Einstein confrontation, some subsequent developments, and an English translation of their agreement to disagree. A side-by-side comparison of two recent summaries of their battle communiques is included to provide an overview of what they had to say on this current issue.

title: The Schwarzschild Proton
content_preview:
Title The Schwarzschild Proton
Read in full Link to paper (Internet Archive)
Author(s) Nassim Haramein
Keywords black holes , Schwarzschild radius, proton, strong force, anomalous magnetic moment
Published 2009
No. of pages 8
Read the full paper here (archived copy — the original link is no longer available)
Abstract
We review our model of a proton that obeys the Schwarzschild condition. We find that only a very small percentage (~10 -39 %) of the vacuum fluctuations available within a proton volume need be cohered and converted to mass-energy in order for the proton to meet the Schwarzschild condition. This proportion is similar to that between gravitation and the strong force where gravitation is thought to be ~10 -40 weaker than the strong force. Gravitational attraction between two contiguous Schwarzschild protons can easily accommodate both nucleon and quark confinement. In this picture, we can treat "strong" gravity as the strong force. We calculate that two contiguous Schwarzschild protons would rotate at c and have a period of 10 -23 s and a frequency of 10 22 Hz which is characteristic of the strong force interaction time and a close approximation of the gamma emission typically associated with nuclear decay. We include a scaling law and find that the Schwarzschild proton falls near the least squares trend line for organized matter. Using a semi-classical model, we find that a proton charge orbiting at a proton radius at c generates a good approximation to the measured anomalous magnetic moment.

Why the third system carries no information

The Ten Assumptions of Science: Toward a New Scientific Worldview is a 2004 book by Glenn Borchardt setting out the philosophical foundation on which his later work — neomechanics , Infinite Universe Theory , the Neomechanical Gravitation Theory and Universal Cycle Theory — is built. It is the shortest and most fundamental of his books, and the one everything else in his programme depends on.
Its argument is that science does not rest on proven absolutes but on assumptions; that every assumption has an equally unprovable opposite; and that most of the confusion in modern physics and cosmology comes from mixing deterministic and indeterministic assumptions without noticing that a choice has been made at all.
Method
Borchardt takes his criteria from the philosopher R. G. Collingwood. A genuinely fundamental assumption has two marks: it always has an opposite, and it can never be completely proven. When more than one is adopted, a third requirement applies — they must be consupponible , meaning that assuming any one of them permits assuming all the others without contradiction.
He presents the ten as satisfying that test as a set, and their indeterministic opposites as forming a rival consupponible set which is the foundation of belief in the supernatural. His claim is not that his assumptions are proven, but that they are coherent, that they are the ones science actually needs, and that the alternatives cannot be held together without contradiction. The assumption of infinity is the thread running through all ten.

The Theory of Gravitation (2007) is a book by the Romanian researcher Sorin Cezar Cosofret , published at Iaşi by Editura Elkadot. It sets out what he calls the theory of planetary vortexes — an account in which the solar system is not a set of bodies moving through empty space under mutual attraction, but a set of bodies moving through a real, moving interplanetary medium which acts on them.
Its most unusual feature is its modesty about what it is attacking. Cosofret states at the outset that the theory is:
not intended as a negation of the Newton's theory of gravitation, but as its complement.
— Sorin Cezar Cosofret, The Theory of Gravitation
The proposal
The argument begins with an observation about what Newtonian celestial mechanics assumes. It:
describes the movement of celestial bodies which constitutes the solar system (planets, comets, asteroids) as in a vacuum, in a completely void, matter less space.
— Sorin Cezar Cosofret, The Theory of Gravitation
That idealisation was reasonable in 1687 and is now known to be false in detail: the space between the planets contains solar wind, dust, plasma and field. Cosofret's move is to ask what follows if that medium is not merely present but in global motion — a vortex.
The consequence is that a planet is subject to two interactions rather than one: the familiar Sun–planet attraction, and an additional interaction between the interplanetary environment and the body moving through it . The second appears in the equations as a corrective term.
The nature of the corrective term
The character of that term is the theory's most carefully stated point, and it is easy to misread. Cosofret specifies that the correction:
refers to the nature (density) of the celestial body, and we may not apply this corrective term to a fundamental interaction.
— Sorin Cezar Cosofret, The Theory of Gravitation

Summary
Roger J Anderton hosted this one himself, and it was aimed less at the mainstream than at his own society. His complaint: if relativity is wrong, there was already a unified theory of everything in place before it, and neither the mainstream nor the dissidents show any interest in going back to it. A hundred people agree Einstein is wrong and produce a hundred private theories instead.
Einstein's point particles
The first half rested on a translation. The commonly used English version of the 1905 paper reads: "Let there be in motion in an electromagnetic field an electrically charged particle (in the sequel called an electron)". Arthur I Miller's translation gives "a point particle possessing electric charge". Anderton put the German passage up and showed that the word rendered simply as "particle" is punktförmiges — point-shaped — so the standard translation drops it.
His inference is that special relativity is a point-particle theory, which he thinks comes as a surprise to many, and that the point-particle tradition runs from Euclid's geometry through Boscovich — and Kant with him — to Einstein. Modern physics is built on it. That, he argued, is why it is no use inventing an alternative mathematics with no connection to Euclidean geometry: the geometry, minus the fifth postulate, is the mathematics classical physics is actually made of, and it gets harder as it develops rather than simpler.

If we were uncovering the truth, I reasoned, then the component parts devised by disparate specialists should dovetail neatly together. But they don't. Classical Newtonian mechanics doesn't see eye-to-eye with Einstein's relativity; both are sneered at by quantum mechanics. Theories highly successful in their own right seemed when compared with one another to be describing different universes.

Title Thermal Momentum in Thermodynamics, Part II Formulation
Author(s) Mahmoud A Melehy
Keywords Momentum, Thermodynamics
Published 1997
Abstract
Forces acting on particles in a thermodynamic system may be diffusive, electric, electromagnetic or gravitationaL It is shown here that, regardless of their nature, such forces can either be motive, or dissipative. Near equilibrium, dissipative forces are locally proportional to the particle flux densities, and lead to Ohm's law, Flick's law, and other dispositive laws, and the Einstein diffusion-mobility/viscosity relation. But particle flux densities are locally indeterminate from motive forces. The interaction of all motive and dispositive forces is governed by a fundamental global relation: the law of conservation of energy, as applied to the entire system. This interaction of all motive and dispositive forces in a system is expressed sufficiently close to equilibrium. It will be shown that at equilibrium, each identifiable, dispositive force, and its corresponding particle flux vanish, and each identifiable motive field, likewise, falls into a state of self-balancing. For, each such force becomes conservative, and the work it does per particle vanishes around every possible closed loop in the system, and, consequently, cannot drive any particle flux. In effect, therefore, at equilibrium, not only the balancing occurs for each constituent, as is the case in classical thermodynamics, but also by each identifiable process. This basic result has interesting ramifications concerning the possible explanation of some mysterious interfacial phenomena to be cited.

He was not a dissident scientist and made no contribution to natural philosophy in the sense documented on this wiki; he appears here for three specific reasons.
The first is Nikola Tesla . Edison employed Tesla in 1884, lost him within a year, and then spent four years fighting the alternating-current system Tesla had designed – and losing. Almost every Tesla source collected on this wiki passes through that episode, and it cannot be read without knowing what Edison actually did and did not do. The second is the Edison effect : in the course of the lamp work Edison observed a current crossing a vacuum, patented it, and set it aside without explanation, leaving the discovery to become the vacuum tube in other hands. The third is his method. Edison worked by exhaustive experiment and was openly contemptuous of mathematical theory – a working style that recurs throughout the independent-research tradition documented here, and one reason his name is invoked so often in it.

Gold's reputation as a Renaissance man was surpassed only by his penchant for unconventional theories -- from the origin of the universe to the source of petroleum. Few scientists ever attempt what Gold made a career of, staking their reputations on ideas that radically challenge the methods and assumptions of an entire discipline.

Tired light is the general name for a family of proposals in which the red shift of light from distant galaxies is caused by a gradual loss of energy by photons as they travel through space, rather than by a recession of the galaxies or an expansion of space. Because a photon's energy is proportional to its frequency, any process that steadily drains energy from light over great distances would lengthen its wavelength — that is, shift it toward the red — by an amount that grows with distance, reproducing the linear redshift–distance relation (Hubble's law) within a static, non-expanding universe . In mainstream physics and astronomy tired light is regarded as an obsolete and falsified idea; on this wiki it is documented as a serious alternative to the expanding-universe interpretation that underlies the Big Bang , and a substantial body of supporting and reviving work is collected in the section below .

The observed fact that light from distant galaxies is shifted toward longer (redder) wavelengths in proportion to their distance is not in dispute. What is disputed is its interpretation . In the standard cosmology the redshift is read as a Doppler-like effect of galaxies receding from us as space expands. Tired-light models instead attribute the redshift to some interaction between the traveling photons and the intervening medium — or to a novel property of light propagation itself — that removes a small, fixed fraction of a photon's energy per unit distance. Topics In Modern Cosmology was a live session presented by Harry Hamlin Ricker on 2 November 2024 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
This presentation will discuss issues in modern cosmology. The ideas of Dark matter, Dark Energy, The Cosmic Microwave background and other topics basic to modern cosmological models will be discussed and critiqued.
Summary
Harry Ricker continued his survey of standard cosmology with the two hypotheses that carry most of its weight, and closed on a conclusion about how the field works rather than about the physics. The session ran without a separate host, with Vladimir S Netchitailo and Nick Percival taking most of the discussion; Ricker's slides did not advance on the audience's screens for the first stretch, so part of the material had to be gone over twice.
Dark matter follows from inflation
Ricker's central point is one rarely put this plainly: dark matter is not primarily an astronomical inference but a requirement of a particle-physics programme. By the mid-1970s the standard model had been consolidated and its architects turned to cosmology; Guth's inflation followed, resolving the monopole problem, the matter–antimatter imbalance and the flatness problem. But inflation makes a definite prediction about the density parameter Ω, and it cannot work unless Ω = 1, whereas luminous matter gives a value far below that. Dark matter is what closes the gap — non-baryonic, smoothly distributed, and cold rather than hot, since hot dark matter would not let galaxies condense.

Author(s) Jean E Burns

Published 2002
Journal Noetic Journal
Volume 3
Number 4
No. of pages 15
Pages 318-329
Abstract
It is shown that a very small change in the initial angle of orientation of a tumbling cube can be detected by a shift in the endpoint of the trajectory after the cube travels a minimum distance. Specifically, if a cube travels forward in the x direction, with s the number of forward steps (tumbles) in the trajectory, the average sideways deviation DY in final position produced by a change in initial angle 0 dq is given by DY = a(s ? s 0 ), where a is the average length of the sideways step during each tumble and s 0 a term which depends logarithmically on 0 dq . It is proposed that the reason cubes (dice) are popular in games of chance is because this ability of the cube trajectory to magnify small changes allows the possibility for mental influence to act. A general outline is given for experiments using traveling cubes which can test for the action of mental influence.
Overview
This is a mechanics paper written in the service of a parapsychological question. Jean E. Burns asks how large a macroscopic effect a very small perturbation applied at the start of a die's trajectory can produce by the time the die comes to rest, and answers with a closed-form estimate: the sideways displacement grows linearly with the number of tumbles once a threshold number of tumbles has been passed, and the threshold depends only logarithmically on the size of the initial perturbation. The point of the exercise is that an influence too small to observe directly — Burns explicitly declines to specify its magnitude, assuming only that it is small — can nonetheless be detected at the end of a long enough trajectory.
The framing acknowledges from the outset that the existence of mental influence is unsettled.

Sergiu Udrea (who publishes under the name Udrea Sergiu ) is a Romanian-born independent researcher based in Montreal, Canada. Born on 1 February 1975, he is the author of a theory in which light is a wave carried by a material aether , set out in his 2011 work New Theory of Light and Aether .
Scientific work
Udrea's starting point is the classical principle that a wave requires a medium: if light is a wave, he argues, it must propagate through something, and that something is the aether . On his account the many properties of light that are otherwise puzzling — and that the relativistic rejection of the aether leaves without a physical picture — should instead follow naturally from the properties of the aether itself.
He requires the aether not merely to carry light but also to support material particles and the interactions between light and matter, and he takes up the classical difficulty of how a transverse wave can propagate within such a medium. The work belongs to the tradition of aether theories that reject the special-relativistic account of light travelling through empty space and seek to restore a physical medium of propagation. It is not accepted by mainstream physics, which since 1905 has dispensed with the luminiferous aether.

Úlpio Nascimento is a Portuguese research engineer, retired from the Laboratório Nacional de Engenharia Civil (National Laboratory for Civil Engineering) in Lisbon. His professional field is the mechanics of deformable materials, and it shapes the physics he went on to write: both of his recorded papers treat space as an elastic medium and reason about it with the tools of continuum mechanics.
The earlier, " On the Trail of the Fresnel's Search for an Aether Wind " (1998), appeared in Apeiron and returns to the nineteenth-century optical experiments — Fresnel's drag coefficient and the searches for a motion of the Earth through the light-carrying medium.
The later and much longer work, " A Quantum Gravity Model Foregoing the Dark Matter " (2007), sets out a complete model. Space is an etherspace : a discrete elastic lattice whose units, the etherons , are electrons and positrons, frictionless among themselves. Material particles are inclusions that deform the lattice, and the elastic energy stored in that deformation is their mass, in accordance with E = mc ²; a moving particle deforms the medium further, and the increase is its kinetic energy. Because the time light takes to cross one etheron is postulated constant however deformed the etheron may be, absolute time is recovered and the Galilean transformation revalidated.

Abstract
A new model of our Universe, called Model Mechanics (MM), has been formulated. Model Mechanics provides solutions to the following problematic cosmological observations:
It was discovered in 1998 that far reached regions of the Universe are in a state of accelerated expansion. This discovery disagrees with the current theory of gravity (General Relativity Theory), which posits that the expansion of the Universe should be slowing down. Model Mechanics predicted the accelerated expansion of these far reached regions of the universe in 1993.
The observed rotational curves of the galaxies disagree with the predictions of GRT. The existence of a dark matter was introduced to explain these anomalous rotational curves. Model Mechanics posits the existence of dark matter in the form of free S-Particles.

Summary
James Keene on possible confounds in the unipolar induction experiments, the latest of a run of sessions on the subject: three by Harry Ricker on Faraday's original experiments and the competing explanations of them, one by Bob Gray applying Weber's electrodynamics, and one by Ian J Cowan , who hosted this one, on Al Kelly 's repetitions. Keene, whose own field is particle physics and quantum mechanics rather than electromagnetism, said the previous speakers had been good enough to force him to put on his thinking cap, and offered questions rather than a conclusion.
The setup and the complaint
The apparatus he took as standard is the one from Cowan's video: a copper disc symmetric about an axis, a cylindrical bar magnet with one pole close to the disc and separated from it by a little air, brush contacts on the shaft and at the rim, and a meter. Spin the disc and a small voltage appears — typically under fifty millivolts.
His opening criticism was methodological. The experiments do not clearly exclude the competing theories — Maxwell's, Faraday's, Weber's and others — and, as far as he could recall from the earlier sessions, the experimentalists do not calculate the millivolts each theory predicts. Using Instruments is a two-page article by Leslee A Kulba , published in 2010 in issue 48 of the Electric Spacecraft Journal , the journal's final double issue. It is the sixth part of the ten-part handbook on perpetual motion and its testing that Kulba, the journal's technical editor, contributed to that issue, and it is the shortest of the ten.
The text of the article has not been recoverable, and this page describes its subject and its place in the series rather than its argument.
The subject
The instrument is part of the circuit
The first thing a meter does is change what it is measuring. A voltmeter draws current through its input impedance; an ammeter inserts a resistance and drops a burden voltage across it; an oscilloscope probe adds capacitance, typically ten to twenty picofarads for a times-one probe, which is enough to load a high-impedance node and round off the edges of the very waveform being examined. A times-ten probe reduces the loading tenfold at the cost of a tenfold reduction in signal.
In a high-impedance or fast circuit these are not refinements. They are the difference between a reading and an artefact, and they are systematic — repeating the measurement will reproduce the error exactly.
Bandwidth and rise time
An instrument reports what it can follow. A meter with a 1 kHz bandwidth presented with a 20 kHz switching waveform reports something, and that something is not the peak, the average or the RMS value. For an oscilloscope the usable rule is that displayed rise time and true rise time combine in quadrature, and that the instrument's own rise time is roughly 0.35 divided by its bandwidth; a scope needs a bandwidth several times the highest frequency of interest before the displayed edge can be trusted.

Valery P. Dmitriyev is a Russian theoretical physicist based in Moscow, affiliated in his published work with Lomonosov Moscow State University. Since the early 1990s he has pursued a single programme: the construction of explicit mechanical analogies, drawn from the mechanics of continuous media, for the equations of quantum physics and electromagnetism.

Dmitriyev's substratum is what the nineteenth century called the vortex sponge — an ideal fluid threaded in all directions by thin, straight vortex filaments — and his method is to identify the equations governing disturbances of that medium with the equations of physics. Three strands recur across his papers.
The elastic model of the physical vacuum. Treating the vacuum as a solid-like medium whose displacement field corresponds to the magnetic vector potential, he recovers the structure of electromagnetism from elasticity. This line was published in Mechanics of Solids in 1992 and developed in Nuovo Cimento A in 1998.
Vortex filaments and the quantum equations. A helical disturbance on a vortex filament, evolving under the local induction approximation of classical vortex dynamics, obeys an equation of Schrödinger form; adding the filament's elastic response produces a Klein–Gordon-like equation. On this reading the wave function is the position vector of a curve rather than an abstract amplitude. Mechanical Analogy for the Wave-Particle: Helix on a Vortex Filament and Mechanical Interpretation of the Klein-Gordon Equation , both published in Apeiron in 2001, set this out.
Turbulent advection and relativistic effects. In a series of papers from 1993 onwards he argues that the effects usually attributed to relativity — and the mass–energy relation in particular — can be recovered from the behaviour of discontinuities advected in a turbulent fluid, work summarised in The Substratum Origin of Relativistic Effects and E=mc2 in the Turbulent Aether

Variable speed of light ( VSL ) is the proposition that the speed of light c is not a universal constant — that it may differ with position, with epoch, with the gravitational potential, with the medium, with direction of travel, or with the motion of the source.
The proposition matters more than it may appear. The constancy of c is the second postulate of special relativity and the foundation on which the Lorentz transformation, time dilation, length contraction and the relativity of simultaneity all rest. If c varies, that structure requires reworking. It is for this reason that VSL is among the most frequently revisited subjects on this wiki, and also why it attracts researchers with otherwise incompatible positions.
VSL is not one theory but several. The label covers proposals that differ profoundly in what they claim, in how respectable they are considered, and in what would count as evidence for them. Distinguishing them is the first task of this article, because arguments against one variety are routinely presented as though they told against all of them.
Why the question is subtle
Two features of the problem make it harder than it looks, and both are worth stating before the varieties are set out.
The metre is defined by c . Since 1983 the metre has been defined as the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second. The speed of light in vacuum is therefore fixed by definition at exactly 299,792,458 m/s, and can no longer be measured — a measurement that appeared to show a different value would be interpreted as a change in the length of the metre, not in c

Abstract
Acceleration is velocity squared by radial distance. The reason for the term velocity squared is explained with the experimental velocity value for Hydrogen molecules moving at 300 kelvin temperature.
The calculation
The paper is a single chain of arithmetic, and every step in it reproduces.
Step 1: the molecular speed
Fernandes takes the mass of the hydrogen molecule as twice the proton mass, m H = 3.34524316 × 10 −27 kg, and sets the kinetic energy at 300 K equal to (3/2) k B T :

This is standard kinetic theory and the value is correct. One terminological point: the paper calls this the "average velocity", but √(3 k B T / m ) is the root-mean-square speed. This purpose of this article is to highlight the various aspects of a dynamic model of gravitational interaction proposed by the author in an earlier paper. A number of interesting results are obtained when the proposed velocity and acceleration dependent inertial induction terms are used in conjunction with an extended version of Mach's principle. Finally, velocity dependent inertial induction can act as a mechanism for the transfer of solar angular momentum, thus explaining the observed distribution of angular omentum. Abstract
We derive the virial theorem for Weber's law applied to gravitation and electromagnetism.
Overview
Virial Theorem for Weber's Law is a four-page research note published in 2004, pp. 67–70. The wiki's infobox names Andre K T Assis ; the paper has three authors — R. S. Mendes and L. C. Malacarne of the Universidade Estadual de Maringá, and Assis of Unicamp, who completed the work under an Alexander von Humboldt fellowship.
Weber's 1846 force law makes the interaction between two particles depend not only on their separation but on the rate at which that separation changes. The interaction energy is
U ij = (k ij /r ij )(1 − ξ ṛ ij ²/2c²)
with k ij = −Gm i m j and ξ = 6 for gravitation, or k ij = q i q j /4πε 0 and ξ = 1 for electromagnetism. The corresponding force carries a term in r̈ as well as ṛ², so the force on a particle depends on its own acceleration.
The authors note that treatments of Weber's law had been confined to one or two bodies, and set out to begin a statistical treatment of the many-body case. They take the standard virial construction — dot Newton's second law with r i , sum over particles, time-average, and use ⟨dA/dt⟩ = 0 for bounded or periodic motion — and apply it to the Weber force.
The result is
⟨U⟩ = −2⟨T⟩
identical in form to the Newtonian virial theorem, with U now Weber's velocity-dependent potential. They close by suggesting applications to plasma physics and to "the formation or stability of the solar system or of galaxies", describing the note as "a first step in this direction".

Abstract
The concept of free will is central to our lives, as we make day-to-day decisions, and to our culture, in our ethical and legal systems. The very concept implies that what we choose can produce a change in our physical environment, whether by pressing a switch to turn out electric lights or choosing a long-term plan of action which can affect many people. Yet volition is not a part of presently known physical laws, and it is not even known whether it exists -- no physics experiments have ever established its presence. (We will use the terms volition and free will synonymously in this article.) The purpose of this article is to make two points: first, that free will cannot be accounted for by presently known physical laws, and second, that if free will exists, any description of its effects in the physical world necessarily would constitute a radical addition to presently known physical laws...

Jean E. Burns, a consciousness researcher writing in the Journal of Consciousness Studies , sets out to establish two propositions and to survey the consequences of holding both. The first is that free will cannot be accounted for by physics as it now stands, since present laws "encompass only determinism and quantum randomness, and neither of these are what is meant by free will." The second is the sharper one: if free will does exist, then any statement of how it produces effects in the physical world would itself be a radical addition to physical law — not a philosophical thesis about the mind, but new physics.

Wallace Kantor (born 1922) is an American experimental physicist, based in San Diego, California, known for a long series of experiments and theoretical papers challenging Einstein's special theory of relativity . He is best remembered for his 1962 claim to have measured a dependence of the speed of light on the motion of its source — a result that would support an emission (ballistic) theory of light against the second postulate of special relativity.
Scientific work
The 1962 moving-source experiment
Kantor's most-cited result is the experiment reported in "Direct First-Order Experiment on the Propagation of Light from a Moving Source" ( Journal of the Optical Society of America , 1962). Using glass plates mounted on a rotating arm between the mirrors of a modified Michelson–Morley interferometer, he reported a first-order fringe shift — on the order of the roughly 2.9 fringes predicted by emission theory — which he interpreted as showing that light passing through the moving glass is re-emitted at speed c relative to the glass rather than to any fixed frame. If correct, the result would contradict the constancy of the speed of light.
The claim was tested and not confirmed. In 1964 H. E. Babcock and T. G. Hyperacute vision experiments demonstrate conclusively that vision initiates in the retina in the form of a wave. When the idea of wave signaling is applied to human vision considerable evidence is cited to show that physical continuity of the image is maintained until it arrives in the cortex as a standing wave. These findings together with well known properties of the nervous system allow the life form to be treated as an ordinary material system approximated by the time-dependent Schroedinger wave equation, with solutions given by superpositions of standing waves. Abstract
This paper sketches a program towards giving a physically realist model of the photon in terms of properties of the electromagnetic field. It is both shown how to rework traditional wave and particle concepts so as to have a unified concept and how parallel electromagnetic fields can be associated with each charged particle. An account of both light propagation and of interactions with matter is sketched. A suggestion is made as to how the account may be able to explain EPR correlations in the case of polarization entanglement. A possible empirical test is also discussed.
Overview
Robert French sets out to give a realist model of the photon — one in which light really is something definite in the world between emission and detection, rather than a probability amplitude with no referent. His method is to abolish the wave/particle distinction by identifying the two: a photon simply is an oscillating electromagnetic field, and he calls the resulting object a "wave-particle." The obstacles to this identification are the familiar ones — particles are localised, waves are spread out; particles are impenetrable and indivisible, waves pass through one another and break into wavelets — and French's strategy is to remove them by changing the geometry of the field rather than the physics.
The change is this. Conventionally the electric field at a point is a single field, obtained by summing the contributions of every charge. French instead assigns each charged source particle its own three-dimensional subspace, these subspaces lying parallel within an overall four-dimensional space that is purely spatial — "not Minkowski spacetime since all of the dimensions are just spatial." Recent data indicate that the law of action between electric current elements proposed by Ampere is notably superior to the Lorentz (Biot-Savart) law in its ability to describe laboratory observations of currents flowing in single circuits. Ampere's law conforms to Newton's third law and thus cannot be covariantly expressed. The virtues of this approach are (a) mathematical simplicity, (b) rigorous conformity to Newton's third law, and (c) agreement with Ampere's law of action between current elements — hence with the observations just mentioned. Two different "modernizations" of Weber's approach are examined, dependent on whether energy or force methods are viewed as more fundamental in mechanics. This eleven-page piece, dated Budapest, 21 April 2006, is a condensed presentation of material from Gyula I. Szász's book Physics of Elementary Processes: Basic Approach in Physics and Astronomy . It is laid out as slides rather than as a continuous paper: three figures, a set of video frames from a drop-tower experiment, and a numbered chain of equations.
Its thesis is that the two foundations of Newtonian gravitation both fail. The gravitational constant G is not constant, and gravitational and inertial mass are not equal — the ratio depends on the composition of the body. From there he proposes a replacement: an elementary, invariant gravitational charge carried by four stable particles, obeying a field equation of Maxwellian form. The departure from the mainstream is total — the equivalence principle is abandoned, the neutron does not appear among the elementary constituents, and gravity becomes a vector field rather than spacetime curvature.

Abstract
The Lorentz force has nothing, either mathematically or physically, to do with Maxwell's field equa-tions. Properly written F L = q( E (1) + v x B (2) ), the Lorentz force is just a phenomenological expression allowing one to describe (parametrically) the motion of a charged particle in the external fields E (1) and B (2) originating from independent sources belonging to different, decoupled systems. Electrodynamics can be built starting from a force-law between moving charges, without separately postulating field equations. There is no need for a "special" relativity theory.

Why Relativity is Wrong - Experimental facts was a live session presented by Hans Deyssenroth on 4 January 2025 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
The Data from the Lunar Laser Ranging Project Contradict Einstein’s Ingenious Spacetime Idea. Why the Theories of Relativity are wrong, though they are usually considered to be right. Experimental facts.
Summary
Hans Deyssenroth — who mentioned in passing that he would turn 88 within three weeks — presented a survey of experiments he takes to contradict relativity, built around one substantial piece of original analysis: a correlation he has found in the return rates of the Lunar Laser Ranging project.
The argument about reflection
The core claim is about what happens when light meets a moving mirror. A tennis ball striking a mirror tilted at 45° acquires momentum in the mirror's direction of travel, so its path becomes oblique. Lorentz and Einstein assumed photons behave the same way, and it is from that oblique path that time dilation is derived by Pythagoras — with length contraction then added to preserve the Michelson–Morley null result.
Deyssenroth's objection follows Feynman: photons are not reflected at a mirror at all. They are absorbed by atoms in the glass and new photons are emitted a short time later. A mirror is therefore a light source — and by Einstein's own second postulate, light propagates independently of the motion of its source. "Why the ‘Cyclic Universe’ is Impossible" is an article by Glenn Borchardt published on 10 November 2025 on The Scientific Worldview .
Borchardt treats the cyclic universe — alternating expansions and contractions — as one of a family of proposals that preserve the expansion interpretation by elaborating it, the multiverse being another. His objection is mechanical: every event in the universe occurs through collision, and any hypothesis requiring events without collisions is false. He allows that recycling occurs, but for portions of the universe rather than the whole of it.

Wolfgang Ernst Pauli (25 April 1900 – 15 December 1958) was an Austrian theoretical physicist, author of the exclusion principle, of the neutrino hypothesis, and of the spin–statistics theorem. He received the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physics "for the discovery of the Exclusion Principle, also called the Pauli Principle."
Pauli was a prodigy: his 237-page encyclopedia article on relativity, written at twenty-one, was praised by Einstein and remained a standard reference for decades. In 1925 he stated the exclusion principle — no two electrons in an atom may share the same set of four quantum numbers — which accounts for the shell structure of atoms and hence for the whole shape of the periodic table. To do so he had to postulate a fourth, two-valued quantum number, shortly afterwards identified as electron spin by Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit. In 1927 he wrote spin into non-relativistic quantum mechanics using the Pauli matrices .
In December 1930, faced with the continuous energy spectrum of beta decay — which appeared to violate conservation of energy — Pauli proposed in an open letter to a conference at Tübingen, addressed to "Dear Radioactive Ladies and Gentlemen," an undetected neutral particle of very small mass carried off in the decay. Fermi named it the neutrino. Pauli called it a desperate remedy and doubted it would ever be detected; it was confirmed by Cowan and Reines in 1956, two years before his death. In 1940 he proved the spin–statistics theorem , connecting half-integer spin to Fermi statistics and integer spin to Bose statistics.

World-Universe Cosmology (WUC) presents a transformative cosmological framework that challenges and revises the standard Big Bang Model (BBM). By addressing and resolving key paradoxes in contemporary cosmology, WUC offers a fresh perspective on the origins, evolution, and structure of the World. Host by Ian Cowan
Summary
Having given eight separate presentations on his framework over the previous year, Vladimir S Netchitailo returned to compress twenty-four years of work into a single hour — a review of World-Universe Cosmology, its principal claims, and the historical lineage he reads it as continuing.
A different kind of eternal universe
WUC rejects the initial singularity. The Universe is eternal and continuously generates new matter, which puts it in the family of steady-state models — Netchitailo quoted Fred Hoyle on obtaining an expanding stationary universe by adding continuous creation to the field equations, without a cosmological constant. But four things distinguish it: a distinct concept of a beginning of the World as opposed to the Universe; a specific mechanism for matter creation; a decreasing energy density; and a four-dimensional geometry.
That geometry is the model's organising idea, and it turns on a distinction Netchitailo pressed hard: stretching, not expansion. The World is the hypersphere — the three-dimensional surface — of a four-dimensional nucleus whose radius grows at c . Expansion, he argued, presupposes a centre; a practically infinite universe has none, so it is unclear what is expanding or into what. Xing-Zhong Li (also published as X. Z. Li or Xing Zhong Li) is a Chinese physicist and professor emeritus in the Department of Physics at Tsinghua University in Beijing, China. He is known internationally for his theoretical and experimental research on Cold Fusion and low-energy nuclear reactions (LENR), and in particular for the selective resonant tunneling model of sub-barrier fusion.
Biography
Li spent his academic career at Tsinghua University in Beijing, where he taught and carried out research in the Department of Physics and later held the title of professor emeritus. He originally worked in conventional ("hot") fusion and plasma physics before turning his attention, after the announcements of 1989, to the anomalous nuclear effects reported in deuterium-loaded metals. Gas-loading experiments to introduce deuterium into palladium lattices have been carried out in his Tsinghua laboratory since 1989.
Scientific contributions
Li is best known for the selective resonant tunneling model, which treats sub-barrier fusion of light nuclei as a resonant tunneling process described by a complex nuclear potential rather than by the conventional compound-nucleus picture. He and his collaborators applied the model both to the established cross-section data of hot fusion reactions and to the principal puzzles raised by cold fusion claims, namely the penetration of the Coulomb barrier, the near-absence of neutron emission, and the near-absence of gamma radiation accompanying the reported excess heat.
On the experimental side, his group at Tsinghua pursued gas-loading of deuterium into palladium as an alternative to electrolytic loading, and reported measurements of anomalous heat and of related nuclear signatures.

Abstract
If anything in modern physics can be said to have attracted the most attention, it is surely the topic of time dilation, along with the associated "twin paradox." Many experiments with varying degrees of precision demonstrate conclusively the phenomenon that moving clocks run slowly. These experiments are here elucidated in enough detail to remove any doubt about the existence of the phenomenon. That said, the question arises whether this means that time is "dilated," or whether "clocks" run slowly simply because they move through the gravitational (or other) field . There is, in fact, a rational basis upon which to decide the question.

Everyone claims to be a critical thinker. Everyone claims that they weigh all the pros and cons. But in reality, no one really does. Summary
David de Hilster 's return to the Saturday sessions after a long absence, and the bluntest talk the society has hosted about itself. title: Yukawa-Type Potential Effects in the Anomalistic Period of Celestial Bodies
content_preview:
Title Yukawa-Type Potential Effects in the Anomalistic Period of Celestial Bodies
Author(s) Ioannis Iraklis Haranas , Omiros Ragos
Keywords celestial mechanics, orbital and rotational dynamics, classical field theories.
Published 2010
No. of pages 10
Abstract
Several contemporary modified models of gravity predict the existence of a non-Newtonian Yukawa-type correction to the classical gravitational potential. We study the motion of a secondary celestial body under the influence of the corrected gravitational force of a primary. We derive two equations to approximate the periastron time rate of change and its total variation over one revolution (i.e., the difference between the anomalistic period and the Keplerian period) under the influence of the non-Newtonian radial acceleration. Kinematically, this influence produces apsidal motion. We performed numerical estimations for Mercury, for the companion star of the pulsar PSR 1913+16, and for the extrasolar Planet b of the star HD 80606. We also considered the case of the artificial Earth satellite GRACE-A, but the results present a low degree of reliability from a practical standpoint.

title: Yukawa-type Effects in Satellites Dynamics

Title Yukawa-type Effects in Satellites Dynamics
Author(s) Ioannis Iraklis Haranas , Omiros Ragos
Keywords Yukawa potential, Lagrange planetary equations, Sagnac interferometry, GRACE mission
Published 2010
Volume Astrophysics and Space Science
No. of pages 7
Abstract
Many of today's gravity theories predict the existence of a non-Newtonian Yukawa-type correction to the gravitational potential. New experimental techniques, such as Sagnac interferometry, can help in exploring the range Lamda > 10 14 , where such forces are possibly measurable. It is expected that future space missions will operate in this range which has not been examined for a very long time. Restricting ourselves to an Earth orbiting satellite we follow a perturbing potential approach applied on the Lagrange planetary equations, in order to study the effect of such a non-Newtonian potential in the range Lamda=1.073 R. This is achieved by calculating the time rates of change of the orbital elements for the earth orbiting satellite GRACE-A. All these time rates have been calculated on the Keplerian and the precessing Keplerian ellipse of the body under study. Of all the orbital elements, the argument of the perigee is most affected by this potential.

Title Betavoltaic Batteries
Author(s) Paul M Brown
Keywords betavoltaic battery, energy beta particles, radioactive source, tritium, electrical power, amorphour silicon cells, nuclear
Published 1999
Pages 41-51
Abstract
A betavoltaic battery is a nuclear battery that converts energy from beta particles released by a beta emitting radioactive source, such as tritium, into electrical power. The application of tritiated amorphous silicon as an intrinsic energy conversion semiconductor for betavoltaic devices is presented. Thin-film contact potential tritiated amorphous silicon cells have been built. These cells, called tritium batteries, have a specific power of 24 watts per kilogram, a full load operating life of 10 years, and an overall efficiency on the order of 25%. Cheap, long-life, high energy density, low power batteries.
The entrapment of tritium is particularly apt in this application as it is readily substituted for the hydrogen present in hydrogenated amorphous semiconductors with good intrinsic electronic properties. Radioisotopes other than tritium, may also be used as a source of energetic electrons as well as other forms of energetic nuclear radiation such as krypton-85 for example.
Tritiated amorphous films are mechanically stable, free of flaking or blistering, with good adherence to the substrate and may be simultaneously deposited onto both conducting and insulating substrates using a discharge in tritium plasma. The silicon layer sputtered in a tritium/argon ambient at temperatures below 300 o C results in a tritiated amorphous silicon firlm with the tritium concentration being variable from 5 to 30% depending upon deposition conditions.

Bill Ramsay (born 1926) is an American independent experimenter based in western Colorado. Across nine papers presented between 1990 and 2008, largely at the International Symposium on New Energy and to the Natural Philosophy Alliance , his work falls into three connected strands: bench measurements of the Rodin coil , a long-running observational technique he calls fixed-rate scanning , and the documentation and testing of Gregory Hodowanec 's Rhysmonic Cosmology and its gravity-wave detectors.
He is unusual in this literature for being an instrument person rather than a theorist. His papers are largely accounts of what a particular piece of apparatus did, and they are consistently explicit about the limits of what was shown.
Rodin coil measurements
Ramsay's two 1995 papers are the most quantitative treatment of the Rodin coil this wiki holds. He obtained a copy of Marko Rodin 's Aerodynamicsss , wound several coils to the design, and measured them against conventionally wound toroids.
" Rodin Coil Design " reports the construction and the first tests. Its framing is candid: Ramsay states plainly that none of his coils matched the proportions Rodin considers necessary for the most significant results, and that his tests, while showing "some interesting attributes and a few surprises", were non-definitive .
" Rodin Coil Test Result Explanations " presents the data — impedance against frequency from 1–10 MHz for several winding configurations, and B-field plots along and across the toroidal axis, each compared with a standard toroid. Perreault is the originator of what he calls the Perreault Atomic Model, a proposed reinterpretation of nuclear structure that he presents as the basis for building radiant-energy power generators. He describes himself as a principal investigator of the early T. H. Moray radiant-energy discoveries and claims to have made a number of related discoveries of his own.
Among the devices he has described are the Perreault Ion Valve (later termed the "star chamber"), which he presents as a controller for a pre-glow discharge in radiant-energy circuits; the "Nu Energy" battery; an ion-capture cell; and a rotary ion-discharge tube. title: Carbon-Arc Gasification of Biomass Solutions
content_preview:
Title Carbon-Arc Gasification of Biomass Solutions
Author(s) David Wallman
Keywords carbon-arc, gasification, biomass, gas, hydrogen, oxide, helium, electrical, energy. voltage, current
Published 1999
Pages 197-212
Abstract
A Biomass Gasification Process converts organic feedstock solutions into a unique, hydrogen-based gas. The Process used forced, rapid oxidation of means of a low voltage, high current DC carbon-arc immersed in an aqueous biomass solution.
Use of direct current forces oxidation of the anode, while carbon from the biomass solution is electroplated onto the cathode. This produces a gas which is an oxide of carbon, in combination with hydrogen. With proper electrical input and control of the carbon-arc, the mass of the carbon electrodes will be maintained through electroplating of the carbon.
Gas chromatography indicates the gas is COH 2 , resembling water gas or synthesis gas. However, the gas (Carbo-hydrogen TM ) possesses unique properties. Analytical testing indicates the gas is stable and may be a compound. Comparative calorimetry shows an energy content of the gas to be 550 BTU/ft3. Ignition of the gas produces water vapor and carbin dioxide. Gas chromatography has also indicated helium in the gas as high as 60 ppm in some samples.
Conversion efficiency measurements for the gas produced show an increase in system enthalpy of at least 27% to 44%, compared to the electrical input energy to the Process. Properties of the gas allow its use as a fuel and a chemical raw material. This Process provides an extraordinary opportunity for use of renewable biomass materials worldwide.

Daniel H. Deutsch (29 August 1922 – 16 November 1997) was an American physicist based in Pasadena, California, who over the last decade of his life developed an alternative account of quantum physics built on two claims: that Planck's constant is a quantum of angular momentum rather than of action, and that elementary particles are physical structures made of rotating massless charges rather than featureless points.
His work was published in Physics Essays and Galilean Electrodynamics , and presented at meetings of the Natural Philosophy Alliance . It is unusual among the material collected here in being a fully constructive programme: rather than arguing chiefly that the standard account is wrong, Deutsch set out to build concrete mechanical models of the photon, electron, proton, neutron and neutrino, and to derive their properties from geometry and motion.
Biography
Deutsch lived and worked in Pasadena, California. He remained active to the end of his life, reading papers at the Natural Philosophy Alliance meeting in San Luis Obispo in July 1997 and at a meeting in Cologne in late August of the same year, only months before his death on 16 November 1997 at the age of 75.
John Chappell , writing in the Alliance's newsletter shortly afterwards, recorded:
Dr. Daniel H. Deutsch of Pasadena, Calif. died in mid-November, just prior to the completion of this newsletter, aged 75. He read carefully-reasoned papers at the San Luis Obispo meeting last July, and then also at the Cologne meeting in late August. He also published in major dissident journals. Cheerful and generous, Dan will be sorely missed.

Don Smith (Don L. Smith) was an American inventor associated with the free-energy movement, known for a large series of Tesla-inspired devices that he claimed could draw usable electrical power from what he called "the ambient background." His designs are widely circulated in the free-energy community, though his over-unity claims are not accepted by mainstream science.
Resonance energy devices
Smith's devices were based on the ideas of Nikola Tesla , and in particular on Tesla's notion of tapping a "radiant" or environmental energy. He said that reading The Inventions, Researches and Writings of Nikola Tesla had led him to reconstruct and then extend Tesla's apparatus, and over the following years he built what supporters count as dozens of different devices.
His designs use resonant induction : a low-voltage source drives a high-voltage stage (typically a neon-sign transformer) feeding tuned coils and capacitors, arranged so the circuit is driven at resonance. Smith claimed that such an arrangement delivers far more energy than it consumes — outputs he described as ranging from kilowatts to megawatts — with the surplus drawn from the surrounding environment rather than from the input battery. He set out his methods in the book Resonance Energy Methods and in a series of public lectures and demonstrations, including a widely circulated 2006 presentation.
A claim of this kind — that a device delivers more energy than is supplied to it — describes an over-unity or perpetual-motion machine, which would violate the conservation of energy. No such device by Smith or others has been independently verified under controlled conditions, and this work is not accepted by mainstream physics.

Experimental Design is a three-page article by Leslee A Kulba , published in 2010 in issue 48 of the Electric Spacecraft Journal , the journal's final double issue. It is the fifth part of the ten-part handbook on perpetual motion and its testing that Kulba, the journal's technical editor, contributed to that issue, and it begins the practical half: having described the machines and the principles, the remaining six articles are about how to find out.
The text of the article has not been recoverable, and this page describes its subject and its place in the series rather than its argument.
The subject
The ordinary requirements
An experiment is a question put in a form that can be answered wrongly. The requirements are the familiar ones and they are not negotiable by subject matter: state in advance what result would count as confirming and what would count as refuting; change one variable at a time; run a control — the same apparatus with the effect deliberately disabled — and check that it gives the null result; record the conditions, not only the readings; and have someone else repeat it with their own equipment.
The last is the one that matters most and is skipped most often. A result that only appears in one shed, on one bench, with one person present, is not yet a result. Independent replication is what distinguishes a discovery from a fault in a particular set-up, and it is unforgiving precisely because the apparatus that produced the anomaly does not travel with it.

From the Archives of Lester J. Hendershot is a 1995 book compiled and self-published by Mark M. Hendershot from the personal papers of his father, the inventor Lester J. Hendershot (1898–1961). It gathers documents, notes, correspondence and photographs relating to the Hendershot fuelless generator — the "magnetic motor" that made Lester Hendershot briefly famous in 1928 — and is one of the principal source collections on the device and the controversy surrounding it.
Overview
Drawing on material Lester Hendershot left behind, the book documents the origin of the fuelless generator (which Hendershot said he stumbled upon while developing a fuelless aviation compass), its public unveiling and the intense press attention it drew, the interest of prominent backers, and the political and commercial difficulties that eventually caused Hendershot to set the work aside. As a first-hand family compilation rather than an independent technical study, it preserves primary material — letters, diagrams and recollections — that would otherwise have been lost, and it remains a key reference within the free-energy community. The device's operation has never been independently verified, and its claimed fuelless output is not accepted by mainstream science.

How Peace Activists Can Be More Effective is an article by Buryl Payne arguing that peace activism could be made more effective by taking account of what he describes as the cyclic, externally-triggered nature of war, and by the deliberate use of collective "thought power." The claims below are the author's own and are not accepted by the scientific mainstream.
Peace activities are all too often reactive rather than proactive. Only after an international battle or war has occurred are attempts made to ameliorate situations by constructing treaties, agreements, or the curtailment of nuclear weapons, cluster bombs, poison gas, biological weapons, and so on. This is political symptom treatment. Historical analysis shows this approach is only partially successful: when wars start up again, peace treaties go out the window. Effective treatment of warring behavior may be aided by a more modern understanding of the nature of war.
Section I. Wars come and go in cycles
Warring behavior can be considered as a kind of mass psychosis — insane behavior. Individuals who behave that way are locked up and treated by psychiatrists.
The most important finding of scientists, based on observations rather than theories, is that wars come and go in cycles. These cycles were discovered by the late Professor Raymond Wheeler, a psychologist and historian at the University of Kansas. As part of his larger historical analysis he found that international battles happen in approximately 11-year cycles, and have done so for 2,500 years. His work was later statistically validated by Edward Dewey, Director of the Foundation for the Study of Cycles, who considered the analysis of war cycles the most important work of his life. A portion of Wheeler's data on war cycles was presented in the article as Figure 1 (an 11⅕-year cycle in international battles, 1760–1947).

Introduction to Error Analysis & Interpretation is a three-page article by Leslee A Kulba , published in 2010 in issue 48 of the Electric Spacecraft Journal , the journal's final double issue. It is the tenth and last part of the handbook on perpetual motion and its testing that Kulba, the journal's technical editor, contributed to that issue, and it closes both the practical sequence and the journal itself.
The text of the article has not been recoverable, and this page describes its subject and its place in the series rather than its argument.
The subject
Two kinds of error
Random errors scatter repeated readings around a value; they are reduced by averaging, and the scatter itself estimates them. Systematic errors displace every reading in the same direction; averaging does nothing to them, they leave no trace in the scatter, and they are found only by changing something about the method — a different instrument, a different technique, a different laboratory. A result can therefore be highly precise and entirely wrong, and the whole of the preceding series is concerned with sources of the second kind: probe loading, average-responding meters, thermoelectric offsets, mismatch, apparent power read as real.
Propagating uncertainty
An uncertainty on a measured quantity implies an uncertainty on anything computed from it. For a sum or difference the absolute uncertainties combine in quadrature; for a product or quotient the relative ones do. Only the first of these is peculiar to this subject, and it is peculiar in a way that matters a great deal.

Scientific career
